course.title: Digital Literacy Essentials
course.subtitle: Use computers, the internet and everyday digital tools with confidence — from your first click to your first professional email.
course.description:
Digital skills are now as important as reading and writing. Whether you want to do better at school, apply for a job, run a small business or simply stay in touch with family, you need to be comfortable with computers and the internet.

This course is designed for complete beginners. Each lesson is short, uses everyday examples from Ghana and beyond, and ends with a small activity you can try right away. By the end, you will be able to use a computer confidently, find reliable information online, communicate professionally by email and keep yourself safe on the internet.
outcomes: Name the main parts of a computer and explain what each one does
Organise files and folders so you can always find your work
Search the internet effectively and judge whether a source is trustworthy
Write and send clear, polite emails with attachments
Protect your accounts with strong passwords and avoid common scams
Use documents, spreadsheets and slides for school and work
requirements: No experience needed — this course starts from zero

lessons.title: What is a computer?
lessons.content:
A **computer** is an electronic machine that accepts information (input), works on it (processing), keeps it (storage) and gives you a result (output). That simple cycle — **input → process → output**, with **storage** alongside — describes every computer, from a giant server to the phone in your pocket.

### Computers are everywhere
You already use more computers than you think:

- A **smartphone** is a small, powerful computer with a touchscreen.
- An **ATM** at the bank is a computer that checks your card and PIN.
- A **mobile money** transaction is handled by computers in a data centre.
- A modern **car** contains dozens of tiny computers that control the engine and brakes.

### Hardware and software
Every computer has two sides:

| | What it is | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Hardware** | The physical parts you can touch | Screen, keyboard, mouse, processor, battery |
| **Software** | The instructions that tell the hardware what to do | Windows, Android, Microsoft Word, WhatsApp, a web browser |

Hardware without software is like a body without thoughts; software without hardware has nowhere to run. They always work together.

### The operating system
The most important software is the **operating system (OS)**. It starts when you switch the device on and manages everything else: files, apps, the screen and the keyboard. Common operating systems are:

- **Windows** and **macOS** on laptops and desktops
- **Android** and **iOS** on phones and tablets
- **Linux**, used on many servers and also on some computers in schools

> [!TIP]
> When someone asks "What computer do you use?", they often mean "What operating system?". Knowing your OS helps you follow instructions and fix problems.

### Types of computers
- **Desktop** — sits on a desk, has a separate monitor, keyboard and mouse. Powerful and easy to repair.
- **Laptop** — portable, with a built-in screen, keyboard and battery.
- **Tablet** — a touchscreen device, lighter than a laptop.
- **Smartphone** — the computer most people in Ghana use every day.
- **Server** — a powerful computer that provides services (websites, email, mobile money) to many users over a network.

> [!TRY]
> Look around your home or classroom. List five devices that contain a computer. For each one, write down one input, one output and whether it stores information.

lessons.title: Inside the computer: input, output, processing and storage
lessons.content:
Let us open the box — not literally! — and see what each part does.

### Input devices
Input devices let you give information to the computer.

- **Keyboard** — for typing letters, numbers and commands
- **Mouse / touchpad** — for pointing, clicking and dragging
- **Touchscreen** — both input (you touch it) and output (it shows pictures)
- **Microphone** — records sound and voice
- **Camera / webcam** — captures pictures and video
- **Scanner** — turns paper documents into digital images

### Output devices
Output devices show or give you the result.

- **Monitor / screen** — displays text, images and video
- **Speakers / headphones** — play sound
- **Printer** — puts documents on paper
- **Projector** — shows the screen on a wall for a class or meeting

### Processing: the CPU
The **Central Processing Unit (CPU)**, also called the **processor**, is the "brain" of the computer. It follows instructions billions of times per second. Processor speed is measured in **gigahertz (GHz)**. A faster processor with more **cores** can do more work at the same time.

### Memory and storage — they are not the same!
This is where many beginners get confused.

| | RAM (memory) | Storage |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | Holds what you are working on *right now* | Keeps files and apps *permanently* |
| When power goes off | Everything is lost | Everything stays |
| Typical size | 4 GB – 16 GB | 128 GB – 1 TB |
| Example | The table where you spread out your books while studying | The shelf where you keep all your books |

Storage comes in two main types:

- **HDD (Hard Disk Drive)** — spinning disks, cheaper, slower
- **SSD (Solid State Drive)** — no moving parts, much faster and more durable

### Units of storage
Computers count in **bytes**. One byte stores roughly one letter.

- 1 **KB** (kilobyte) ≈ 1,000 bytes — a short text message
- 1 **MB** (megabyte) ≈ 1,000 KB — a photo from a phone (2–5 MB)
- 1 **GB** (gigabyte) ≈ 1,000 MB — about an hour of standard video
- 1 **TB** (terabyte) ≈ 1,000 GB — hundreds of movies

> [!NOTE]
> When you buy a data bundle, it is measured in the same units. A 1 GB bundle can stream roughly one hour of standard-quality video — which is why downloading courses for offline study saves you money.

> [!TRY]
> On a computer, open **Settings → System → About** (Windows) or **Settings → About phone** (Android). Write down your device's RAM and storage.

lessons.title: Mastering the keyboard and mouse
lessons.content:
Good keyboard and mouse skills make everything faster. Professionals rarely hunt for keys — they use shortcuts and type without looking.

### Using the mouse
- **Click** (left button once) — select something
- **Double-click** — open a file or program
- **Right-click** — show a menu of options for that item
- **Click and drag** — move items or select text
- **Scroll wheel** — move up and down a page

On a laptop **touchpad**, tap with one finger to click and tap with two fingers to right-click.

### Important keys
- **Shift** — type capital letters and the top symbol on a key (e.g. `Shift + 2 = @`)
- **Caps Lock** — turns capital letters on and off
- **Enter** — start a new line or confirm
- **Backspace** — delete the character to the *left* of the cursor
- **Delete** — delete the character to the *right* of the cursor
- **Tab** — jump to the next box in a form
- **Esc** — cancel or close

### Shortcuts that save hours
Hold the first key, then press the second.

| Shortcut (Windows) | Mac | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `Ctrl + C` | `Cmd + C` | Copy |
| `Ctrl + X` | `Cmd + X` | Cut |
| `Ctrl + V` | `Cmd + V` | Paste |
| `Ctrl + Z` | `Cmd + Z` | Undo your last action |
| `Ctrl + S` | `Cmd + S` | Save |
| `Ctrl + F` | `Cmd + F` | Find a word on the page |
| `Ctrl + A` | `Cmd + A` | Select all |
| `Alt + Tab` | `Cmd + Tab` | Switch between open programs |

> [!TIP]
> `Ctrl + Z` (undo) is your best friend. Deleted a paragraph by mistake? Press `Ctrl + Z` immediately.

### Typing properly
Place your fingers on the **home row**: left hand on `A S D F`, right hand on `J K L ;`. Feel the small bumps on `F` and `J` — they help you find the home row without looking. Each finger is responsible for the keys above and below its home key.

Start slowly and focus on accuracy. Speed comes with practice. A good goal for students is **30–40 words per minute** with few mistakes.

> [!TRY]
> Practise for 10 minutes a day on a free typing site such as Typing.com (see the Resource library). Record your words-per-minute today and again after one week.

lessons.title: Files and folders explained
lessons.content:
Everything you save on a computer — a letter, a photo, a song — is a **file**. To keep files tidy, we put them into **folders** (also called *directories*), just like papers in a cabinet.

### File names and extensions
A file name has two parts separated by a dot: `report.docx`

- `report` is the **name** you choose.
- `.docx` is the **extension**, which tells the computer what *type* of file it is and which program should open it.

| Extension | Type | Opens with |
|---|---|---|
| `.docx` | Word document | Microsoft Word, Google Docs, LibreOffice |
| `.xlsx` | Spreadsheet | Excel, Google Sheets |
| `.pptx` | Presentation | PowerPoint, Google Slides |
| `.pdf` | Portable document | Any PDF reader or web browser |
| `.jpg`, `.png` | Images | Photos app, browser |
| `.mp3` | Audio | Music player |
| `.mp4` | Video | Video player |
| `.zip` | Compressed folder | File manager (extract first) |

> [!WARNING]
> Be very careful with files ending in `.exe`, `.apk` or `.bat` that arrive by email or WhatsApp. These are programs, and opening them can install viruses.

### Paths: the address of a file
A **path** shows exactly where a file lives, like an address:

```
C:\Users\Ama\Documents\School\SHS1\Maths-assignment.docx
```

Read it from left to right: drive `C:` → `Users` → `Ama` → `Documents` → `School` → `SHS1` → the file.

### Good naming habits
- Use clear, descriptive names: `CV-Kwame-Mensah-2026.pdf`, not `final final 2.pdf`
- Use dashes or underscores instead of spaces for files you will share online
- Put dates as **year-month-day** (`2026-03-15`) so files sort in order
- Avoid symbols like `/ \ : * ? " < > |` — many systems do not allow them

> [!TRY]
> Create a folder called `DBI Learn` in your Documents. Inside it, create folders called `Notes`, `Projects` and `Certificates`. This is where you'll keep your work for this programme.

lessons.title: Organising, finding and backing up your work
lessons.content:
A tidy computer saves time and stress. Professionals follow a simple system.

### A simple folder structure
```
Documents/
├── School/
│   ├── 2026-Term1/
│   └── 2026-Term2/
├── Work/
│   ├── CV-and-applications/
│   └── Projects/
└── Personal/
    ├── Photos/
    └── Receipts/
```
Keep the top level small (3–6 folders). Go deeper only when a folder gets crowded.

### Moving, copying and deleting
- **Copy** (`Ctrl + C`, then `Ctrl + V`) makes a duplicate; the original stays.
- **Cut** (`Ctrl + X`, then `Ctrl + V`) moves the file.
- **Delete** sends a file to the **Recycle Bin** (Windows) or **Trash** (Mac). You can restore it from there until you empty the bin.
- **Drag and drop** with the mouse moves files between folders on the same drive.

### Finding files fast
- Use the **search box** in File Explorer or the Start menu and type part of the name.
- Sort a folder by **Date modified** to see your newest work first.
- On Android, use the **Files** app and its search.

### Back up — or risk losing everything
Laptops get stolen, phones fall into water, and hard drives fail. A **backup** is a second copy kept somewhere else.

The professional rule is **3-2-1**:

- **3** copies of important files,
- on **2** different types of storage (e.g. laptop + flash drive),
- with **1** copy off-site or in the cloud (e.g. Google Drive, OneDrive).

**Cloud storage** keeps your files on secure servers on the internet. Google gives every account 15 GB free. Files sync automatically between your phone and computer, and you can share a link instead of attaching large files.

> [!TIP]
> Turn on automatic photo backup in Google Photos or OneDrive so your pictures are saved even if you lose your phone.

> [!TRY]
> Copy your three most important files to a flash drive *or* upload them to Google Drive. Congratulations — you now have a backup.

lessons.title: Compressing and sharing files
lessons.content:
Large files are slow to send and use a lot of data. Compression and smart sharing help.

### Compressing with ZIP
A **ZIP** file packs many files into one smaller file.

- **Windows:** select the files → right-click → **Send to → Compressed (zipped) folder**.
- **Mac:** select → right-click → **Compress**.
- To open a zip, double-click it, then choose **Extract all** so you can edit the files.

Zipping text documents can reduce their size a lot. Photos and videos are already compressed, so zipping them saves little.

### Choosing the right format to share
- Send **PDF** when you want the document to look the same everywhere and not be edited — CVs, certificates, final reports.
- Send **DOCX/XLSX** when the other person needs to edit.
- Reduce photo size before sending: most phones let you choose "standard" instead of "original" quality.

### Sharing a link instead of an attachment
Email attachments are usually limited to about 20–25 MB. For bigger files, upload to Google Drive or OneDrive and share a link. You can choose who can **view**, **comment** or **edit**.

> [!WARNING]
> "Anyone with the link" means exactly that — anyone who gets the link can open the file. Use it only for things that are not private.

> [!TRY]
> Save one of your documents as a PDF (in Word: **File → Save As → PDF**; in Google Docs: **File → Download → PDF**). Compare the file sizes.

lessons.title: How the internet and the web work
lessons.content:
The **internet** is a worldwide network of computers connected by cables, satellites and radio signals. The **World Wide Web** is one service that runs on the internet — the websites you visit in a **browser** such as Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari. Email, WhatsApp and video calls also use the internet but are not "the web".

### How you connect
- **Mobile data** (3G/4G/5G) from MTN, Telecel or AirtelTigo
- **Wi-Fi** from a router at home, school or a café
- **Fibre / fixed broadband** in offices

### Web addresses (URLs)
A URL is the address of a page:

```
https://www.ghana.gov.gh/education/scholarships
```

- `https://` — the **protocol**. The **s** means *secure* (encrypted). Look for the padlock 🔒 in the address bar.
- `www.ghana.gov.gh` — the **domain name**. `.gov.gh` is used by government; `.edu.gh` by schools; `.com` by companies.
- `/education/scholarships` — the specific **page** on that site.

> [!WARNING]
> Scammers create look-alike domains such as `mtn-promo-gh.com` or `ecobank-verify.net`. Always check the real domain before entering passwords or payment details.

### Using a browser well
- **Tabs** let you keep several pages open; `Ctrl + T` opens a new tab.
- **Bookmarks** (`Ctrl + D`) save pages you visit often.
- **History** (`Ctrl + H`) shows pages you visited before.
- **Incognito/private mode** does not save history on that device — useful on shared computers, but it does *not* make you invisible online.

> [!TRY]
> Open your browser, bookmark the DBI Learn website, then open a new tab with `Ctrl + T` and close it with `Ctrl + W`.

lessons.title: Searching smartly and checking sources
lessons.content:
Search engines like Google and Bing can find almost anything — if you ask well. And because anyone can publish online, you must check what you find.

### Search like a pro
- Use **specific keywords**, not full questions: `WASSCE 2026 timetable` instead of "when will the WASSCE exams start this year please".
- Put exact phrases in **quotes**: `"climate change in Ghana"`
- Exclude words with a minus sign: `jaguar -car`
- Search one website: `scholarships site:edu.gh`
- Find a file type: `business plan template filetype:pdf`

### Is this source trustworthy? Use the **CRAAP** test
- **Currency** — When was it published or updated? Old information may be wrong today.
- **Relevance** — Does it actually answer your question?
- **Authority** — Who wrote it? Are they an expert, a government body, a recognised organisation?
- **Accuracy** — Is it supported by evidence? Do other reliable sources agree?
- **Purpose** — Is it trying to inform, sell something, or make you angry so you share it?

### Spotting fake news
Be suspicious when a message:
- uses ALL CAPS, many exclamation marks or says "forward to 10 people",
- promises free money, free data or a job with no interview,
- has no named source or date,
- uses edited or old photos (try a reverse image search with Google Lens).

> [!TIP]
> Before you share, pause and check. Search the headline and see whether trusted news outlets are reporting the same thing.

> [!TRY]
> Search for "benefits of drinking water". Pick two results and score each one against the CRAAP test. Which one would you use for a school assignment, and why?

lessons.title: Writing professional emails
lessons.content:
Email is the main way schools, employers and organisations communicate. A well-written email makes a strong first impression.

### Create a professional address
Use your name: `kofi.boateng@gmail.com` — not `sweetboy4life@...`. Gmail and Outlook are free.

### Parts of an email
- **To** — the main recipient
- **Cc** (carbon copy) — people who should be informed
- **Bcc** (blind carbon copy) — hidden recipients; use it when emailing many people who don't know each other
- **Subject** — a short, clear summary
- **Body** — your message
- **Attachment** 📎 — files you send along

### A professional email template
```
Subject: Application for IT Assistant Internship – Kofi Boateng

Dear Mrs. Asante,

I am writing to apply for the IT Assistant internship advertised on your
website. I am a final-year SHS student and have completed the Digital
Literacy and Web Development courses on DBI Learn.

Please find my CV and certificate attached. I would welcome the
opportunity to discuss how I can support your team.

Thank you for your time.

Kind regards,
Kofi Boateng
+233 24 000 0000
```

### Golden rules
1. Write a **specific subject**.
2. Greet properly: "Dear Mr./Mrs./Dr. Surname" or "Hello Ama" for people you know.
3. Keep it **short** — say why you're writing in the first two lines.
4. **Attach before you write** "please find attached" — it's easy to forget!
5. Re-read for spelling and tone before you click **Send**.
6. Reply within 24–48 hours when someone writes to you.

> [!WARNING]
> Never send your passwords, PINs or mobile-money codes by email. No genuine bank, school or company will ask for them.

> [!TRY]
> Write an email to a teacher or mentor asking for advice on which DBI Learn course to take next. Use the template above.

lessons.title: Passwords, 2-step verification and scams
lessons.content:
Your email and social media accounts are keys to your digital life. If someone steals your email password, they can reset the passwords of almost everything else.

### Make passwords strong — and different
A strong password is **long** and **unique**. The easiest way is a **passphrase**: several random words together.

- Weak: `ama123`, `password`, `12345678`, your birthday
- Strong: `Mango-Bicycle-Rain-47!`

Never reuse the same password on different sites. If one site is hacked, criminals try that password everywhere. A **password manager** (such as Bitwarden or the one built into Chrome/Google) can remember them for you.

### Turn on 2-step verification (2SV)
**Two-step verification** asks for a second proof — a code sent to your phone or an authenticator app — after your password. Even if someone steals your password, they cannot get in without your phone. Turn it on for email, WhatsApp, Facebook and banking apps.

> [!TIP]
> In WhatsApp, go to **Settings → Account → Two-step verification** and set a PIN. This stops criminals from taking over your account.

### Common scams in Ghana and how to spot them
- **Mobile money reversal scam:** "I sent money to your number by mistake, please send it back." Check your actual MoMo balance — usually no money arrived.
- **Fake promotions:** "You've won GH₵5,000! Send your PIN to claim." Real promotions never ask for your PIN.
- **Phishing links:** messages pretending to be from your bank or school with a link to "verify your account".
- **Job scams:** jobs that ask you to pay a "registration fee" first.

**The golden rule:** never share your PIN, password or one-time code with anyone — not even someone who says they are from MTN, the bank or DBI.

> [!TRY]
> Change the password of your main email to a passphrase and switch on 2-step verification today.

lessons.title: Documents, spreadsheets and presentations
lessons.content:
Three types of "office" programs cover most school and work tasks. Free options include **Google Docs/Sheets/Slides** (online, with offline mode), **Microsoft 365 web** and **LibreOffice** (free download).

### Word processors — for writing
Use **Word** or **Google Docs** for letters, essays, CVs and reports.

- Use **Heading 1 / Heading 2** styles for titles — this lets you create an automatic table of contents.
- Use **bullet points** for lists.
- Insert **page numbers** and use **spell check** (red underlines).
- Export to **PDF** before sending final versions.

### Spreadsheets — for numbers and lists
Use **Excel** or **Google Sheets** for budgets, marks, inventories and data. A spreadsheet is a grid of **cells** named by column letter and row number (`B3`). You can write **formulas** that calculate automatically:

```
=SUM(B2:B10)      adds the numbers from B2 to B10
=AVERAGE(C2:C30)  finds the average mark
```

You'll go much deeper in our **Spreadsheets & Data Analysis** course.

### Presentations — for sharing ideas
Use **PowerPoint** or **Google Slides** for class presentations and pitches. Follow the **1–6–6 rule**: one idea per slide, no more than six bullet points, no more than six words per bullet. Use large images and few words — you are the presenter, not the slides.

> [!TIP]
> Google Docs, Sheets and Slides save automatically and let several people edit the same file at once — perfect for group assignments.

> [!TRY]
> Create a one-page document introducing yourself: your name, school, three skills you want to learn, and your dream job. Use a heading and a bullet list, then download it as a PDF.

lessons.title: Healthy, responsible digital habits
lessons.content:
Technology should help you, not harm you. Good digital citizens protect their health, their privacy and other people.

### Your digital footprint
Everything you post online leaves a **digital footprint**. Employers and universities often search applicants' names. Before posting, ask: *Would I be happy for my teacher, parent or future boss to see this?*

- Set social media accounts to **private** if you don't need them public.
- Don't post your exact location, school timetable or home address.
- Think twice before sharing photos of other people — ask permission.

### Respect and online kindness
Treat people online as you would face to face. **Cyberbullying** — insulting, threatening or embarrassing someone online — causes real harm. If you are bullied: don't reply, take screenshots, block the person and tell a trusted adult or teacher.

### Copyright and plagiarism
Copying someone else's work and presenting it as your own is **plagiarism**. Always credit sources, and use images that are free to use (for example from Unsplash or Pexels).

### Look after your body
- Follow the **20-20-20 rule**: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
- Sit with your back supported and the screen at eye level.
- Avoid screens for an hour before bed — sleep matters for learning.

> [!TRY]
> Search your own name on Google. What would a stranger learn about you? Is there anything you'd like to make private?

keys.explanation: A printer produces a result (paper) from the computer, so it is output. The others send information into the computer.
RAM is temporary working memory and is cleared when power goes off. Storage (HDD/SSD) keeps files permanently.
Ctrl + Z is "undo". Ctrl + X is cut and Ctrl + S is save.
The Central Processing Unit follows instructions and does the calculations — the "brain" of the computer.
Android is an operating system — a set of instructions. The others are physical hardware.
Microphones, webcams and touchscreens send information into the computer. Speakers and projectors are output devices.
1 gigabyte is roughly 1,000 megabytes. (Strictly 1,024, but 1,000 is a good rule of thumb.)
Your index fingers rest on F and J; the bumps let you find them without looking.
The extension shows the file type. `.xlsx` is an Excel spreadsheet.

lessons.title: Welcome to the grid
lessons.content:
A **spreadsheet** is a grid made of **rows** (numbered 1, 2, 3…) and **columns** (lettered A, B, C…). Where a row and column meet is a **cell**, named by its column then row: **B3** is column B, row 3. A file is called a **workbook**, and each tab at the bottom is a **worksheet** (or sheet).

### Why spreadsheets matter
- **Automatic calculations** — change one number and every total updates.
- **Organisation** — thousands of rows of data in a neat table.
- **Analysis** — sort, filter, summarise and chart in seconds.
- **Everywhere** — Excel, Google Sheets and LibreOffice Calc all work the same way.

### Finding your way around
- The **Name Box** (top-left) shows the selected cell's address.
- The **Formula Bar** shows what is really inside the cell — a number, text or formula.
- A **range** is a block of cells written with a colon: `A1:C10` means from A1 down to C10.
- `Ctrl + Arrow key` jumps to the edge of your data; `Ctrl + Home` returns to A1.

### Types of data
| Type | Example | Tip |
|---|---|---|
| Text | `Kumasi`, `Product name` | Left-aligned by default |
| Number | `250`, `12.5` | Right-aligned by default — never type "GH₵" inside the number |
| Date | `15/03/2026` | Stored as a number, so you can calculate with it |
| Formula | `=B2*C2` | Always starts with `=` |

> [!TIP]
> If a number is left-aligned, the spreadsheet may be treating it as text. That often happens when you copy data from the web or type a space before it.

> [!TRY]
> Open a new spreadsheet. In A1 type **Item**, in B1 **Quantity**, in C1 **Price (GH₵)**. Add five items you might buy at the market with quantities and prices.

lessons.title: Entering and formatting data like a pro
lessons.content:
Good structure makes everything later — formulas, charts, analysis — much easier.

### The golden rules of a data table
1. **One header row** with a clear name for each column.
2. **One record per row** (e.g. one sale, one student).
3. **One type of data per column** — don't mix numbers and notes.
4. **No blank rows or columns** in the middle of your data.
5. **Don't merge cells** inside a data table — it breaks sorting and filtering.

### Speed tricks
- **AutoFill:** type `Monday` in a cell, then drag the small square at its bottom-right corner (the *fill handle*) to fill the rest of the week. Works for numbers like 1, 2, 3 and dates too.
- **Flash Fill (Excel):** type an example of the pattern you want (e.g. first names from full names) and press `Ctrl + E`.
- `Ctrl + ;` inserts today's date.
- `Alt + Enter` starts a new line inside the same cell.

### Formatting for readability
- **Number formats:** use *Currency* or *Accounting* for money, *Percentage* for rates, and set decimal places consistently.
- **Bold the header row** and use **Freeze Panes** (*View → Freeze Top Row*) so headers stay visible as you scroll.
- **Format as Table** (Excel `Ctrl + T`) adds banded rows, filters and makes formulas easier.
- Keep colours simple: one highlight colour for headers, one for warnings.

> [!WARNING]
> Formatting changes how a number *looks*, not its value. A cell showing `GH₵ 3` might actually contain `2.6`. Use the ROUND function when you need the value itself rounded.

> [!TRY]
> Turn your market list into a proper table: bold headers, currency format on the Price column, freeze the top row and apply *Format as Table*.

lessons.title: Your first formulas
lessons.content:
Formulas make spreadsheets powerful. Every formula starts with an **equals sign (=)**.

### Arithmetic operators
| Operator | Meaning | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+` | Add | `=5+3` | 8 |
| `-` | Subtract | `=10-4` | 6 |
| `*` | Multiply | `=6*7` | 42 |
| `/` | Divide | `=20/4` | 5 |
| `^` | Power | `=2^3` | 8 |

The spreadsheet follows **BODMAS**: brackets first, then powers, then multiply/divide, then add/subtract. `=2+3*4` is 14, but `=(2+3)*4` is 20.

### Use cell references, not typed numbers
Instead of `=5*12`, write `=B2*C2`. Now if the quantity in B2 changes, the result updates automatically.

For our market list, add a column **D: Total** and in D2 type:

```
=B2*C2
```

Press **Enter**, then drag the fill handle down. The formula adjusts for each row: D3 becomes `=B3*C3`, D4 becomes `=B4*C4`. This is called a **relative reference**.

### Absolute references with $
Sometimes one cell must stay fixed. Suppose a 15% VAT rate is in cell **G1**. In E2 you want `=D2*G1`. If you drag it down, E3 would become `=D3*G2` — wrong! Lock the reference with dollar signs:

```
=D2*$G$1
```

`$G$1` is an **absolute reference**: it never changes when copied. Press **F4** after typing a reference to add the `$` signs automatically.

> [!TIP]
> `$G1` locks only the column; `G$1` locks only the row. These *mixed references* are handy for multiplication tables and grids.

> [!TRY]
> Put `0.15` in G1 with the label "VAT rate" in F1. Add a column **VAT** that calculates `=D2*$G$1` and a **Grand total** column `=D2+E2`. Fill both down.

lessons.title: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT
lessons.content:
A **function** is a ready-made formula. You write its name followed by **arguments** in brackets: `=FUNCTION(arguments)`.

### The big five
Suppose a teacher has test scores for 30 students in **B2:B31**.

| Function | Example | What it gives |
|---|---|---|
| `SUM` | `=SUM(B2:B31)` | Total of all scores |
| `AVERAGE` | `=AVERAGE(B2:B31)` | The mean score |
| `MIN` | `=MIN(B2:B31)` | Lowest score |
| `MAX` | `=MAX(B2:B31)` | Highest score |
| `COUNT` | `=COUNT(B2:B31)` | How many cells contain numbers |

Related counters:
- `COUNTA` counts cells that are **not empty** (text too) — useful for counting names.
- `COUNTBLANK` counts empty cells — useful to see who hasn't submitted.

### AutoSum shortcut
Select the cell just below a column of numbers and press **Alt + =**. Excel guesses the range and writes the SUM for you.

### Rounding
- `=ROUND(B2, 1)` rounds to 1 decimal place.
- `=ROUNDUP` and `=ROUNDDOWN` always go up or down.

### The status bar
Select any range and look at the bottom of the window: Excel shows the **Sum, Average and Count** instantly — no formula needed. Great for quick checks.

> [!TIP]
> Functions ignore empty cells and text when calculating SUM and AVERAGE. A student who was absent (blank) does not pull the average down — but a 0 does. Decide which you mean!

> [!TRY]
> Create a mark sheet with 10 students and 3 subjects. Add a **Total** column using SUM and an **Average** row using AVERAGE. Find the highest and lowest total with MAX and MIN.

lessons.title: Making decisions with IF
lessons.content:
The **IF** function lets the spreadsheet make a decision:

```
=IF(logical_test, value_if_true, value_if_false)
```

### Pass or fail
If a score in B2 of 50 or more is a pass:

```
=IF(B2>=50, "Pass", "Fail")
```

### Comparison operators
| Operator | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `=` | equal to |
| `<>` | not equal to |
| `>` / `<` | greater than / less than |
| `>=` / `<=` | greater than or equal / less than or equal |

Text must be in double quotes: `=IF(C2="Paid", 0, D2)`.

### Grading with nested IF or IFS
To award grades A–F you can nest IFs, but **IFS** (Excel 2019+, Google Sheets) is easier to read:

```
=IFS(B2>=80,"A", B2>=70,"B", B2>=60,"C", B2>=50,"D", TRUE,"F")
```

The final `TRUE` acts as "everything else".

### Combining conditions with AND / OR
- `=IF(AND(B2>=50, C2>=50), "Promoted", "Repeat")` — both conditions must be true.
- `=IF(OR(D2="Absent", D2=""), "Follow up", "OK")` — either can be true.

> [!WARNING]
> A common mistake is typing curly “smart quotes” copied from Word. Spreadsheets only accept straight quotes `"`.

> [!TRY]
> Add a **Grade** column to your mark sheet using IFS, and a **Status** column that says "Promoted" only if the average is 50 or more *and* no subject is below 40.

lessons.title: COUNTIF, SUMIF and XLOOKUP
lessons.content:
These three functions answer most everyday business questions.

### COUNTIF — "how many…?"
```
=COUNTIF(range, criteria)
=COUNTIF(E2:E31, "Pass")        how many passed
=COUNTIF(B2:B31, ">=80")        how many scored 80 or more
```

### SUMIF — "how much for…?"
A shop records sales with the product in column B and amount in column D:

```
=SUMIF(B2:B500, "Rice", D2:D500)
```

adds all sales amounts where the product is Rice. For several conditions use **SUMIFS**:

```
=SUMIFS(D2:D500, B2:B500, "Rice", C2:C500, "Accra")
```

(Note that in SUMIFS the sum range comes *first*.) There is also **COUNTIFS** and **AVERAGEIF(S)**.

### XLOOKUP — find information in a table
Suppose a price list has product names in **A2:A50** and prices in **B2:B50**. To find the price of the product typed in E2:

```
=XLOOKUP(E2, A2:A50, B2:B50, "Not found")
```

It reads: *look up E2, in the list A2:A50, return the matching value from B2:B50; if there is no match, show "Not found".*

If your version doesn't have XLOOKUP, use **VLOOKUP**:

```
=VLOOKUP(E2, A2:B50, 2, FALSE)
```

`2` means "return the 2nd column" and `FALSE` means "exact match only". Always use FALSE unless you know why you need TRUE.

> [!TIP]
> Lookups fail when there are extra spaces: "Rice " is not the same as "Rice". Wrap values in `TRIM()` to clean them.

> [!TRY]
> Build a small price list of 8 products. On another sheet, type a product name and use XLOOKUP (or VLOOKUP) to show its price automatically.

lessons.title: Sorting and filtering
lessons.content:
Large tables are only useful if you can find what you need.

### Sorting
Select any cell inside your table and use **Data → Sort**.

- **A → Z** sorts text alphabetically; **Smallest → Largest** sorts numbers.
- Use **Custom Sort** to sort by more than one column — for example by *Region* and then by *Sales* from largest to smallest.

> [!WARNING]
> Never select just one column and sort it — the rest of the row stays behind and your data gets scrambled. Click one cell inside the table, or select the whole table, then sort.

### Filtering
**Data → Filter** (or `Ctrl + Shift + L`) adds drop-down arrows to each header. You can:

- tick only the values you want to see (e.g. only "Kumasi"),
- use **Number Filters** such as *Greater Than 1000* or *Top 10*,
- use **Text Filters** such as *Contains "rice"*,
- filter by colour.

Filtering **hides** rows; it doesn't delete them. The row numbers turn blue to remind you. Clear the filter to see everything again.

### SUBTOTAL for filtered data
`SUM` adds hidden rows too. To total only the *visible* rows after filtering, use:

```
=SUBTOTAL(9, D2:D500)
```

(9 means SUM; 1 means AVERAGE; 3 means COUNTA.)

> [!TRY]
> Using a sales table, filter to show only one region, then use SUBTOTAL to show that region's total sales.

lessons.title: Cleaning messy data
lessons.content:
Real-world data is messy: extra spaces, inconsistent spelling, duplicates and numbers stored as text. Analysts often spend most of their time cleaning. Clean data = trustworthy results.

### Common problems and fixes
| Problem | Example | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Extra spaces | `" Accra "` | `=TRIM(A2)` |
| Inconsistent capitals | `accra`, `ACCRA` | `=PROPER(A2)` → `Accra` |
| Joined data | `Mensah, Kofi` | **Data → Text to Columns** split by comma |
| Separate first & last names | `Kofi` + `Mensah` | `=A2&" "&B2` or `=TEXTJOIN(" ",TRUE,A2,B2)` |
| Duplicate rows | same sale entered twice | **Data → Remove Duplicates** |
| Numbers as text | `'250` | `=VALUE(A2)` or *Convert to Number* |
| Spelling variations | `Kumasi`, `Kumase` | Find & Replace (`Ctrl + H`) |

### Text functions worth knowing
- `=LEFT(A2, 3)` — first 3 characters (e.g. a product code prefix)
- `=RIGHT(A2, 4)` — last 4 characters
- `=LEN(A2)` — number of characters (find phone numbers with the wrong length!)
- `=UPPER(A2)` / `=LOWER(A2)`

### Work on a copy
Always keep the original raw data on its own sheet. Do your cleaning in new columns or a copy. Then if something goes wrong, you can start again.

> [!TIP]
> After cleaning with formulas, **Copy → Paste Special → Values** to replace formulas with their results before deleting the original columns.

> [!TRY]
> Type a list of 10 town names with mixed capitals and extra spaces. Use `=PROPER(TRIM(A2))` to clean them all in one step.

lessons.title: Data validation and conditional formatting
lessons.content:
Prevent mistakes before they happen, and make important values stand out.

### Data validation: control what people can type
Select a range and go to **Data → Data Validation**.

- **List** — create a drop-down (e.g. `Paid, Unpaid, Partial`). This stops spelling variations.
- **Whole number between** 0 and 100 — perfect for test scores.
- **Date** after a certain day.
- Add an **input message** to guide users and an **error alert** to block wrong entries.

Drop-down lists are one of the simplest ways to keep shared spreadsheets clean.

### Conditional formatting: let colour tell the story
**Home → Conditional Formatting** changes a cell's look based on its value.

- **Highlight Cells Rules** — e.g. scores below 50 in red.
- **Top/Bottom Rules** — highlight the top 10%.
- **Data Bars** — mini bar charts inside cells.
- **Color Scales** — green-to-red heat maps.
- **Icon Sets** — arrows or traffic lights.

You can also use a formula rule. To highlight the whole row of any student who failed, select the table and use the rule:

```
=$E2="Fail"
```

The `$` locks column E, so every column in the row checks the same Status cell.

> [!WARNING]
> Don't overuse colour. If everything is highlighted, nothing stands out. Choose one or two rules that answer a real question.

> [!TRY]
> Add a drop-down list to a "Payment status" column and use conditional formatting to colour "Unpaid" rows light red.

lessons.title: PivotTables — summaries in seconds
lessons.content:
A **PivotTable** summarises thousands of rows without a single formula. It is the most powerful tool most people never learn — and employers love it.

### When to use one
You have a sales table with columns **Date, Region, Product, Salesperson, Amount**. You want to know:
- total sales per region,
- which product sells best in each region,
- monthly sales trends.

### Creating a PivotTable
1. Click any cell inside your table.
2. **Insert → PivotTable** (Google Sheets: **Insert → Pivot table**).
3. Choose **New Worksheet** and click OK.
4. In the field list, drag fields into four areas:

| Area | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Rows** | Categories down the side | Region |
| **Columns** | Categories across the top | Product |
| **Values** | Numbers to summarise | Sum of Amount |
| **Filters** | Filter the whole report | Salesperson |

Instantly you get a grid of total sales for each region and product.

### Useful tricks
- Click the Values field → **Value Field Settings** to switch between Sum, Count, Average, Max.
- Right-click a date in Rows → **Group** → *Months* to see monthly totals.
- **Show Values As → % of Grand Total** shows each region's share.
- When the source data changes, right-click the PivotTable → **Refresh**.

> [!TIP]
> Format your source data as a Table (`Ctrl + T`) before creating the PivotTable. New rows you add later will be included automatically when you refresh.

> [!TRY]
> Create a sales table with at least 20 rows (Region, Product, Amount). Build a PivotTable showing total sales per region, then add Product to Columns.

lessons.title: Choosing and building the right chart
lessons.content:
A good chart shows the answer at a glance. A bad chart confuses. The secret is choosing the right type for your question.

### Pick the chart for the question
| Question | Best chart |
|---|---|
| How do categories compare? | **Column** or **bar** chart |
| How has something changed over time? | **Line** chart |
| What share does each part make up of a whole? (few parts) | **Pie** or **doughnut** chart |
| Is there a relationship between two numbers? | **Scatter** chart |
| What is the distribution of values? | **Histogram** |

Use a **bar** chart (horizontal) when category names are long, such as school names.

### Building a chart
1. Select your data including headers.
2. **Insert → Recommended Charts** (or choose a type).
3. Add a clear **chart title** that states the insight, e.g. "Kumasi had the highest sales in March".
4. Label the axes and remove clutter (heavy gridlines, 3-D effects, unnecessary legends).

### Design rules for honest charts
- Start bar and column charts at **zero** — otherwise small differences look huge.
- Use **one highlight colour** for the bar you want people to notice and grey for the rest.
- Sort bars from largest to smallest unless there's a natural order (like months).
- Avoid pie charts with more than five slices.

> [!WARNING]
> 3-D charts look impressive but distort sizes and make values harder to read. Professionals avoid them.

> [!TRY]
> From your PivotTable, insert a column chart of sales by region. Give it a title that tells the reader the main finding.

lessons.title: Project — build a personal budget dashboard
lessons.content:
Let's combine everything into a practical tool: a monthly budget in Ghana cedis.

### Step 1: The transactions sheet
Create a sheet called **Transactions** with columns:

`Date | Description | Category | Type | Amount (GH₵)`

- **Category:** use a drop-down list — *Food, Transport, Data & airtime, School, Savings, Rent, Other*.
- **Type:** a drop-down with *Income* or *Expense*.
- Format it as a Table and enter at least 15 transactions.

### Step 2: The summary sheet
On a sheet called **Summary**:

```
Total income     =SUMIFS(Transactions[Amount (GH₵)], Transactions[Type], "Income")
Total expenses   =SUMIFS(Transactions[Amount (GH₵)], Transactions[Type], "Expense")
Balance          =B1-B2
Savings rate     =IF(B1=0, 0, B4/B1)
```

(If you didn't format as a Table, use normal ranges like `E2:E200`.)

Then list each category in column A and calculate spending per category with SUMIFS.

### Step 3: Make it visual
- Add a **bar chart** of spending by category, sorted largest to smallest.
- Use **conditional formatting** to turn the Balance cell red if it is below zero.
- Add a cell that says `=IF(B3<0, "⚠ Overspending!", "✓ On track")`.

### Step 4: Reflect
Look at your biggest category. Is there one change that could help you save GH₵50 next month? This is exactly how analysts work: **data → insight → action**.

> [!TIP]
> In Google Sheets you can share the budget with a family member and edit it together — and use it offline on your phone.

> [!TRY]
> Complete the dashboard and save it in your `DBI Learn/Projects` folder. It's a great example to show in an interview.

Dollar signs before both the column and row make an absolute reference.
Brackets are calculated first: 5 × 4 = 20.
Cell addresses are column letter followed by row number.
Clean, consistent tables can be sorted, filtered and analysed reliably.

F4 cycles through absolute, mixed and relative references.
COUNTIF counts the cells in the range that meet the criterion.
49 is not greater than or equal to 50, so the "false" value is returned.
FALSE forces an exact match, which is what you want for names and codes.
SUMIF handles one condition; SUMIFS handles one or more.
COUNT only counts numbers; COUNTA counts any non-empty cell.
SUBTOTAL ignores rows hidden by a filter; SUM includes them.
TRIM removes extra spaces and PROPER capitalises each word.
Filtering only hides rows. Clearing the filter shows them again.
A validation list allows only the exact options you define.
Sorting one column alone separates values from the rest of their row.
Line charts show change over time clearly.
Numeric fields go in Values, where they are summed, counted or averaged.
PivotTables must be refreshed (right-click → Refresh) to pick up changes.
Honest axes and clear titles help readers; 3-D and crowded pies make charts harder to read.
Dividing by zero causes a #DIV/0! error; the IF returns 0 instead.
C2 is relative and moves to C10; $F$1 is absolute and stays fixed.
COUNTA counts any non-empty cell.
SUMIF(range to check, criteria, range to add).

lessons.title: How websites work
lessons.content:
When you type `www.example.com` into a browser and press Enter, a lot happens in less than a second:

1. Your browser asks a **DNS server** (the internet's phone book) for the **IP address** of `example.com` — something like `93.184.216.34`.
2. The browser sends a **request** over the internet to the **web server** at that address.
3. The server sends back a **response**: files of HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images.
4. Your browser reads those files and **renders** (draws) the page on your screen.

This is called the **client–server** model. Your browser is the *client*; the computer storing the website is the *server*.

### The three languages of the web
| Language | Job | Analogy (a house) |
|---|---|---|
| **HTML** — HyperText Markup Language | Structure and content | The walls, rooms and doors |
| **CSS** — Cascading Style Sheets | Appearance and layout | The paint, furniture and decoration |
| **JavaScript** | Behaviour and interactivity | The electricity — lights, switches, the doorbell |

### Front end and back end
- **Front-end** developers build what users see in the browser (HTML, CSS, JavaScript).
- **Back-end** developers build the server side: databases, logins, payments (with languages like Python, PHP, Node.js).
- **Full-stack** developers do both.

### Tools you need
- A **browser** — Chrome or Firefox, with built-in **Developer Tools** (press `F12`).
- A **code editor** — VS Code is free and popular. On a phone or shared computer you can use **CodePen.io** in the browser.

> [!TIP]
> Right-click any web page and choose **View page source** to see its HTML. Every website is a learning resource!

> [!TRY]
> Open any website, press `F12`, and click the **Elements** tab. Hover over the code and watch parts of the page highlight.

lessons.title: Forms
lessons.content:
Forms collect information from visitors: sign-ups, contact messages, orders, surveys.

```html
<form action="/subscribe" method="post">
  <label for="name">Full name</label>
  <input type="text" id="name" name="name" required>

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required placeholder="you@example.com">

  <label for="track">Which track interests you?</label>
  <select id="track" name="track">
    <option>Web development</option>
    <option>Data analysis</option>
    <option>Graphic design</option>
  </select>

  <label for="message">Message</label>
  <textarea id="message" name="message" rows="4"></textarea>

  <label><input type="checkbox" name="updates"> Send me updates</label>

  <button type="submit">Send</button>
</form>
```

### Useful input types
`text`, `email`, `password`, `number`, `tel`, `date`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `file`, `range`, `color`. On phones, `type="email"` and `type="tel"` show the right keyboard automatically.

### Labels matter
Always connect a `<label>` to its input with matching `for` and `id`. Clicking the label focuses the input, and screen readers announce what each field is for.

### Built-in validation
- `required` — the field can't be empty.
- `minlength`, `maxlength` — text length.
- `min`, `max` — number range.
- `pattern` — a format rule.

The browser checks these before sending. (Servers must still check everything again — never trust the browser alone.)

### Radio buttons
Radio buttons with the same `name` form a group where only one can be chosen:

```html
<input type="radio" id="m" name="level" value="beginner"><label for="m">Beginner</label>
<input type="radio" id="i" name="level" value="intermediate"><label for="i">Intermediate</label>
```

> [!TRY]
> Build a "Join our coding club" form with name, email, age (number 10–25), preferred day (radio buttons) and a submit button.

lessons.title: CSS basics — selectors, colours and fonts
lessons.content:
CSS is written as **rules**. Each rule has a **selector** (what to style) and **declarations** (how to style it): ```css h1 { color: #0b7be8; font-size: 2.5rem; } ``` ### Adding CSS to your page The best way is an external stylesheet. Create `style.css` and link it inside ``: ```html ``` ### Selectors ```css p { } /* every

element */ .card { } /* every element with class="card" */ #header { } /* the one element with id="header" */ nav a { } /* elements inside

*/ a:hover { } /* links when the mouse is over them */ ``` Use **classes** for most styling — you can reuse them on many elements: `
`. ### Colours ```css color: green; /* named colour */ color: #03c14b; /* hex code */ color: rgb(3, 193, 75); /* red, green, blue */ background-color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.5); /* with 50% transparency */ ``` Make sure text has enough **contrast** against its background so everyone can read it. ### Typography ```css body { font-family: "Inter", Arial, sans-serif; font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.6; color: #1f242d; } ``` - List backup fonts after a comma in case the first isn't available. - `line-height` of 1.5–1.7 makes paragraphs much easier to read. - Free web fonts are available from Google Fonts. ### Units - `px` — fixed pixels. - `rem` — relative to the root font size (1rem = 16px by default). Great for scalable designs. - `%` — relative to the parent element. - `vw` / `vh` — percentage of the screen width/height. ### The cascade When several rules target the same element, CSS decides which wins by **specificity** (id > class > element) and **order** (later rules win). That's the "cascading" in Cascading Style Sheets. > [!TRY] > Create `style.css`, link it to your page, and set a font, a text colour, and a coloured `h1`. Add a hover colour to your links.

lessons.title: The box model and spacing
lessons.content:
Every element on a web page is a rectangular **box**. Understanding this box is the key to layout.

```
┌─────────────── margin ───────────────┐
│  ┌──────────── border ────────────┐  │
│  │  ┌───────── padding ────────┐  │  │
│  │  │         content          │  │  │
│  │  └──────────────────────────┘  │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

- **Content** — the text or image.
- **Padding** — space *inside* the border, around the content.
- **Border** — a line around the padding.
- **Margin** — space *outside* the border, separating it from other elements.

```css
.card {
  padding: 24px;
  border: 1px solid #d5dae2;
  border-radius: 16px;
  margin: 16px 0;
  background: white;
}
```

### Shorthand values
- `margin: 10px;` — all four sides.
- `margin: 10px 20px;` — top/bottom 10px, left/right 20px.
- `margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;` — top, right, bottom, left (clockwise).

### box-sizing: the one rule everyone uses
By default, padding and border are *added* to an element's width, which makes sizes confusing. Add this to the top of every stylesheet:

```css
*, *::before, *::after {
  box-sizing: border-box;
}
```

Now `width: 300px` means the whole box is 300px.

### Centring a block
```css
.container {
  max-width: 1100px;
  margin: 0 auto;     /* auto left/right margins centre it */
  padding: 0 16px;
}
```

### Block vs inline
- **Block** elements (`div`, `p`, `h1`, `section`) start on a new line and take full width.
- **Inline** elements (`a`, `strong`, `span`, `img`) sit inside a line of text.

> [!TIP]
> Open Developer Tools (`F12`), select an element and look at the **box model diagram** in the Styles panel. It shows exact margin, border and padding sizes.

> [!TRY]
> Wrap your page content in `<div class="container">` and style it to be centred with a maximum width. Turn your skills list into a `.card`.

lessons.title: Layout with Flexbox and Grid
lessons.content:
Modern CSS gives us two powerful layout tools. ### Flexbox — for one direction (a row *or* a column) ```css .navbar { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; /* spread along the main axis */ align-items: center; /* centre on the cross axis */ gap: 16px; /* space between items */ } ``` ```html
Ama.dev
About Projects Contact
``` Key Flexbox properties: - `flex-direction: row | column` - `justify-content: flex-start | center | space-between | space-around` - `align-items: stretch | center | flex-start | flex-end` - `flex-wrap: wrap` — let items move to the next line - `flex: 1` on a child — let it grow to fill space ### CSS Grid — for two directions (rows *and* columns) ```css .projects { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 24px; } ``` `1fr` means "one fraction of the free space", so `repeat(3, 1fr)` creates three equal columns. An even better version automatically fits as many columns as there is room for: ```css .projects { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr)); gap: 24px; } ``` On a wide screen you get four columns; on a phone, one — with no extra code! ### Which should I use? - **Flexbox:** navigation bars, buttons in a row, centring things, small components. - **Grid:** whole-page layouts, card galleries, anything with rows and columns. They work together — a grid of cards, each card using flexbox inside. > [!TIP] > To centre anything perfectly inside a box: `display: grid; place-items: center;` > [!TRY] > Create a "Projects" section with six cards in a responsive grid using `repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr))`. Resize your browser and watch the columns adapt.

lessons.title: Responsive design and media queries
Accessibility and semantic HTML
lessons.content:
An **accessible** website works for everyone — including people who are blind, have low vision, are deaf, or can't use a mouse. It's also better for search engines and for everyone on a slow phone.

### Use semantic elements
Instead of building everything with `<div>`, use elements that describe their purpose:

```html
<header>Site logo and navigation</header>
<nav>Main links</nav>
<main>
  <section id="about">...</section>
  <article>A blog post or project</article>
</main>
<aside>Related information</aside>
<footer>Contact and copyright</footer>
```

Screen readers let users jump straight to `<nav>` or `<main>`, and search engines understand your page better.

### Accessibility checklist
- ✅ Every image has meaningful `alt` text (use `alt=""` for purely decorative images).
- ✅ Text has strong colour contrast.
- ✅ Every form input has a `<label>`.
- ✅ Links describe where they go — "Download the timetable", not "click here".
- ✅ You can use the whole site with the **Tab** key; focused elements are visible.
- ✅ Use real `<button>` elements for actions, not clickable `<div>`s.
- ✅ Set `lang="en"` on the `<html>` tag.

### Performance is accessibility too
Many visitors are on mobile data. Keep pages light: compress images, avoid huge background videos, and use system or few web fonts.

> [!TIP]
> In Chrome Developer Tools, the **Lighthouse** tab scores your page for performance, accessibility, best practices and SEO, and tells you exactly what to fix.

> [!TRY]
> Replace the `<div>`s in your page with semantic elements and run a Lighthouse accessibility audit. Aim for a score above 90.

lessons.title: Project — publish your portfolio website
lessons.content:
Time to put it all together and go live! A portfolio website shows employers and clients who you are and what you can do.

### What to include
1. **Header & navigation** — your name/logo and links to sections.
2. **Hero section** — a photo, your name, a one-line summary ("Aspiring front-end developer from Ayeldu, Ghana").
3. **About** — a short paragraph about you and your goals.
4. **Skills** — a list or set of badges (HTML, CSS, Excel…).
5. **Projects** — cards with an image, title, short description and link for each project.
6. **Certificates** — link to your verified DBI Learn certificates.
7. **Contact** — email link, phone and a simple contact form or social links.
8. **Footer** — copyright and a "back to top" link.

### Folder structure
```
portfolio/
├── index.html
├── style.css
└── images/
    ├── profile.webp
    └── project-1.webp
```

### Publishing for free
Several services host static websites for free:

- **GitHub Pages** — create a free GitHub account, create a repository named `yourusername.github.io`, upload your files, and your site is live at `https://yourusername.github.io`.
- **Netlify Drop** or **Cloudflare Pages** — drag and drop your project folder into the website and get a live link in seconds.

### Before you launch: checklist
- [ ] All links work and open the right pages
- [ ] Images have alt text and are compressed
- [ ] It looks good on a phone (test in the device toolbar *and* on a real phone)
- [ ] No spelling mistakes — ask a friend to read it
- [ ] The `<title>` and a `<meta name="description">` are set

> [!TIP]
> Share your live link in your CV, on LinkedIn and in the DBI Learn discussions. Real projects impress employers far more than a list of skills.

> [!TRY]
> Build and publish your portfolio. Post the link in the course discussion so classmates can give you feedback.

lessons.title: What is programming?
lessons.content:
A **program** is a list of instructions that a computer follows exactly. **Programming** (or *coding*) is the skill of writing those instructions in a language the computer understands.

Computers are fast but extremely literal. If you tell a friend "make tea", they know what to do. A computer needs every step: boil water, put tea bag in cup, pour water, wait three minutes, remove bag. Breaking a problem into precise steps is called an **algorithm**, and it's the heart of programming.

### Why Python?
- **Readable** — Python code looks almost like English.
- **Versatile** — websites, data analysis, automation, games, artificial intelligence.
- **In demand** — one of the most requested skills in tech job adverts.
- **Free** — and runs on Windows, Mac, Linux and even Android.

### How Python runs your code
You write code in a file ending in `.py`. The **Python interpreter** reads it line by line, from top to bottom, and carries out each instruction.

### Setting up
**Option 1 — online (no installation):** open an online Python editor such as Programiz, type code on the left and press **Run**.

**Option 2 — on your computer:**
1. Download Python 3 from python.org and install it. On Windows, tick **"Add Python to PATH"**.
2. Install **VS Code** and the Python extension.
3. Create a file `hello.py`, write your code, and run it with the ▶ button or by typing `python hello.py` in the terminal.

> [!TIP]
> On an Android phone, apps such as Pydroid 3 let you write and run Python offline.

> [!TRY]

lessons.title: Your first program: print and comments
lessons.content:
Tradition says every programmer's first program prints a greeting:

```python
print("Hello, world!")
```

Run it, and you'll see `Hello, world!` in the output. Congratulations — you're a programmer!

### The print function
`print()` displays whatever you put inside the brackets.

```python
print("Welcome to DBI Learn")
print("I am learning Python")
print(5 + 3)
print("Total:", 250)
```

Output:
```
Welcome to DBI Learn
I am learning Python
8
Total: 250
```

- Text must be inside quotes — single `'...'` or double `"..."`. Text in quotes is called a **string**.
- Numbers don't need quotes, and Python can calculate with them.
- Commas let you print several things separated by a space.

### Comments
Lines starting with `#` are **comments** — notes for humans that Python ignores.

```python
# This program greets the user
print("Akwaaba!")  # "Welcome" in Twi
```

Good comments explain *why* you did something, not what is obvious.

### Errors are normal
If you write `print("Hello)` (missing a quote), Python shows a **SyntaxError**. Read the message — it tells you the line number and what went wrong. Every programmer sees errors every day; fixing them is part of the job.

> [!TIP]
> Python is **case-sensitive**: `print` works, `Print` does not.

> [!TRY]
> Write a program that prints your name, your school and your favourite food on three separate lines, with a comment at the top explaining what it does.

lessons.title: Variables and data types
lessons.content:
A **variable** is a named box that stores a value so you can use it later.

```python
name = "Esi"
age = 16
height = 1.62
is_student = True

print(name, "is", age, "years old")
```

The `=` sign means **assign** — "put this value in this box". It is not the same as "equals" in maths.

### The main data types
| Type | Name | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| `str` | string (text) | `"Accra"`, `'Hello'` |
| `int` | integer (whole number) | `25`, `-3`, `0` |
| `float` | decimal number | `3.14`, `12.5` |
| `bool` | Boolean | `True`, `False` |

Use `type()` to check: `print(type(age))` shows `<class 'int'>`.

### Naming rules
- Use letters, numbers and underscores, but don't start with a number.
- No spaces: use `first_name`, not `first name`.
- Choose meaningful names: `price_per_bag` is better than `x`.
- Python style uses **snake_case** (lowercase with underscores).

### Doing maths
```python
price = 12.5
quantity = 4
total = price * quantity     # 50.0

print(10 / 3)    # 3.333...  division
print(10 // 3)   # 3          whole-number division
print(10 % 3)    # 1          remainder (modulo)
print(2 ** 5)    # 32         power
```

### Working with strings
```python
first = "Kwame"
last = "Mensah"
full = first + " " + last            # joining strings
print(full.upper())                   # KWAME MENSAH
print(len(full))                      # 12 characters
print(f"Welcome, {first}!")           # f-string: Welcome, Kwame!
```

**f-strings** (put `f` before the quote) let you insert variables inside `{}` — the cleanest way to build messages.

> [!TRY]
> Create variables for an item name, its price in cedis and the quantity. Calculate the total and print a receipt line using an f-string, e.g. `3 x Bread = GH₵ 24.0`.

lessons.title: Getting input from the user
lessons.content:
Programs become interactive when they ask the user for information. The `input()` function shows a message and waits for the user to type something.

```python
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(f"Nice to meet you, {name}!")
```

### input() always returns a string
This catches every beginner out:

```python
age = input("How old are you? ")
print(age + 1)     # TypeError! You can't add a number to a string
```

Convert the input to the type you need:

```python
age = int(input("How old are you? "))
print(f"Next year you will be {age + 1}")

price = float(input("Price in cedis: "))
```

- `int()` converts to a whole number.
- `float()` converts to a decimal.
- `str()` converts a number to text.

### A simple calculator
```python
print("=== Simple shop calculator ===")
item = input("Item: ")
price = float(input("Price per unit (GH₵): "))
qty = int(input("Quantity: "))
total = price * qty
print(f"{qty} x {item} = GH₵ {total:.2f}")
```

`{total:.2f}` formats the number with exactly two decimal places — perfect for money.

> [!WARNING]
> If the user types "ten" instead of "10", `int()` crashes with a ValueError. We'll learn to handle this gracefully in Module 4.

> [!TRY]
> Write a program that asks for the length and width of a room in metres and prints its area with two decimal places.

lessons.title: Conditions with if, elif and else
lessons.content:
Programs often need to choose between options. Python uses `if`, `elif` (else if) and `else`.

```python
score = int(input("Enter your score: "))

if score >= 50:
    print("You passed! 🎉")
else:
    print("Keep practising — you'll get there.")
```

### Indentation matters
The lines that belong to an `if` must be **indented** (4 spaces is standard). Python uses indentation instead of brackets to group code. Wrong indentation causes an `IndentationError` or, worse, a program that runs but does the wrong thing.

### Comparison operators
`==` equal to, `!=` not equal to, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=`

> [!WARNING]
> `=` assigns a value; `==` compares two values. Writing `if score = 50:` is an error.

### Multiple choices with elif
```python
if score >= 80:
    grade = "A"
elif score >= 70:
    grade = "B"
elif score >= 60:
    grade = "C"
elif score >= 50:
    grade = "D"
else:
    grade = "F"
print(f"Your grade is {grade}")
```

Python checks each condition in order and runs only the **first** one that is true.

### Combining conditions
- `and` — both must be true
- `or` — at least one must be true
- `not` — reverses True/False

```python
age = 17
has_permission = True

if age >= 18 or has_permission:
    print("You can join the trip.")
```

> [!TRY]
> Write a program that asks for a temperature in °C and prints "Hot" (above 30), "Warm" (20–30) or "Cool" (below 20).

lessons.title: Loops with for and while
lessons.content:
Loops repeat code so you don't have to write it many times.

### for loops — repeat a set number of times
```python
for i in range(5):
    print("Practice makes progress!")
```

`range(5)` produces the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Variations:

```python
for n in range(1, 11):        # 1 to 10
    print(n, "x 7 =", n * 7)  # the 7 times table

for n in range(0, 101, 10):   # 0, 10, 20 ... 100
    print(n)
```

### Looping over text and lists
```python
for letter in "DBI":
    print(letter)

towns = ["Accra", "Kumasi", "Tamale", "Ho"]
for town in towns:
    print(f"Hello, {town}!")
```

### while loops — repeat until a condition changes
```python
balance = 100
while balance > 0:
    print(f"Balance: GH₵ {balance}")
    balance = balance - 30
print("Out of money!")
```

A `while` loop is useful when you don't know in advance how many times to repeat, such as "keep asking until the user types the right password".

```python
password = ""
while password != "akwaaba":
    password = input("Password: ")
print("Access granted")
```

> [!WARNING]
> If the condition never becomes false, you get an **infinite loop** that runs forever. Make sure something inside the loop changes the condition. Press `Ctrl + C` to stop a runaway program.

### break and continue
- `break` exits the loop immediately.
- `continue` skips to the next repetition.

### Building a total with a loop
```python
total = 0
for day in range(1, 8):
    sales = float(input(f"Sales on day {day}: "))
    total += sales          # same as total = total + sales
print(f"Weekly sales: GH₵ {total:.2f}")
```

> [!TRY]
> Write a program that prints the multiplication table for any number the user chooses, from 1 to 12.

lessons.title: Writing your own functions
lessons.content:
A **function** is a named block of code that does one job. You've already used built-in functions like `print()`, `input()` and `len()`. Now you'll write your own.

```python
def greet(name):
    print(f"Akwaaba, {name}! Welcome to DBI Learn.")

greet("Yaw")
greet("Abena")
```

- `def` starts the definition.
- `name` is a **parameter** — a placeholder for the value you pass in.
- `"Yaw"` is an **argument** — the actual value.
- The indented lines are the function's **body**.

### Returning values
Use `return` to send a result back:

```python
def calculate_total(price, quantity):
    return price * quantity

bill = calculate_total(12.5, 4)
print(bill)   # 50.0
```

A function that returns a value can be used in calculations, `if` statements and other functions.

### Default parameters
```python
def add_vat(amount, rate=0.15):
    return amount * (1 + rate)

print(add_vat(100))         # 115.0 (uses the default 15%)
print(add_vat(100, 0.2))    # 120.0
```

### Why functions matter
- **Reuse** — write once, use many times.
- **Readability** — `calculate_total(...)` explains itself.
- **Testing** — check one small piece at a time.
- **Fewer bugs** — fix a problem in one place.

A good rule: if you copy and paste the same code three times, turn it into a function.

> [!TIP]
> Variables created inside a function exist only inside it (this is called **local scope**). To get a value out, `return` it.

> [!TRY]
> Write a function `grade(score)` that returns "A", "B", "C", "D" or "F", then call it for five different scores.

lessons.title: Lists — storing many values
lessons.content:
A **list** stores an ordered collection of items in a single variable.

```python
subjects = ["Maths", "English", "Science", "ICT"]
scores = [78, 64, 85, 92]
```

### Accessing items by index
Python counts from **0**:

```python
print(subjects[0])     # Maths
print(subjects[2])     # Science
print(subjects[-1])    # ICT (negative counts from the end)
print(subjects[1:3])   # ['English', 'Science'] — a slice
```

### Changing lists
```python
subjects.append("French")       # add to the end
subjects.insert(1, "Twi")       # insert at position 1
subjects.remove("English")      # remove by value
last = subjects.pop()           # remove and return the last item
subjects[0] = "Mathematics"     # replace an item
```

### Useful list functions
```python
scores = [78, 64, 85, 92]
print(len(scores))              # 4
print(sum(scores))              # 319
print(max(scores), min(scores)) # 92 64
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))# average: 79.75
scores.sort()                   # [64, 78, 85, 92]
print(85 in scores)             # True
```

### Looping through a list
```python
for subject, score in zip(subjects, scores):
    print(f"{subject}: {score}")
```

Or with positions using `enumerate`:

```python
for i, subject in enumerate(subjects, start=1):
    print(i, subject)
```

> [!TRY]
> Ask the user for five test scores, store them in a list with `append`, then print the highest, lowest and average score.

lessons.title: Dictionaries — data with labels
lessons.content:
A **dictionary** stores **key–value pairs**, like a real dictionary stores words and their meanings.

```python
student = {
    "name": "Kofi Asante",
    "age": 15,
    "school": "Ayeldu JHS",
    "subjects": ["Maths", "ICT"],
}

print(student["name"])          # Kofi Asante
student["age"] = 16             # update
student["email"] = "kofi@example.com"   # add a new key
```

### Safe lookups
`student["phone"]` crashes with a **KeyError** if the key doesn't exist. Use `.get()` to provide a default:

```python
phone = student.get("phone", "Not provided")
```

### Looping through a dictionary
```python
prices = {"rice": 45.0, "oil": 38.5, "sugar": 22.0}

for item, price in prices.items():
    print(f"{item.title()}: GH₵ {price:.2f}")
```

### Lists of dictionaries — real-world data
Most real data looks like a list of records:

```python
students = [
    {"name": "Ama", "score": 82},
    {"name": "Kojo", "score": 67},
    {"name": "Efua", "score": 91},
]

for s in students:
    status = "Pass" if s["score"] >= 50 else "Fail"
    print(f"{s['name']}: {s['score']} ({status})")

best = max(students, key=lambda s: s["score"])
print("Top student:", best["name"])
```

This is exactly how data from websites and apps (JSON) is structured.

### Choosing the right structure
- **List** — an ordered collection of similar items (scores, names).
- **Dictionary** — labelled information about one thing (a student's details), or a lookup table (prices).

> [!TRY]
> Create a dictionary of five products and their prices. Ask the user for a product name and print its price, or "Sorry, we don't sell that" if it isn't there.

lessons.title: Understanding and handling errors
lessons.content:
Errors aren't failures — they're messages telling you what to fix.

### Reading an error message (traceback)
```
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "shop.py", line 4, in <module>
    total = price * qty
NameError: name 'qty' is not defined
```

Read from the **bottom up**: the last line tells you the error type and message; the line above shows where it happened.

### Common errors
| Error | Meaning | Typical fix |
|---|---|---|
| `SyntaxError` | Python can't understand the code | Check brackets, quotes and colons |
| `IndentationError` | Wrong spacing | Use 4 spaces consistently |
| `NameError` | A variable doesn't exist | Check spelling; define it first |
| `TypeError` | Wrong type, e.g. `"5" + 3` | Convert with `int()` or `str()` |
| `ValueError` | Right type, bad value, e.g. `int("ten")` | Validate input |
| `IndexError` | List position doesn't exist | Check the list length |
| `KeyError` | Dictionary key doesn't exist | Use `.get()` |
| `ZeroDivisionError` | Dividing by zero | Check before dividing |

### Handling errors with try / except
```python
try:
    age = int(input("Your age: "))
    print(f"In 10 years you'll be {age + 10}")
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter your age as a number, e.g. 16")
```

Python *tries* the code; if a `ValueError` happens, it runs the `except` block instead of crashing.

### Keep asking until the input is valid
```python
while True:
    try:
        qty = int(input("Quantity: "))
        if qty > 0:
            break
        print("Quantity must be more than zero.")
    except ValueError:
        print("That's not a whole number. Try again.")
```

> [!TIP]
> Catch specific errors (`except ValueError:`) rather than everything (`except:`). Catching everything hides real bugs.

> [!TRY]
> Update your shop calculator so it never crashes, no matter what the user types.

lessons.title: Debugging strategies
lessons.content:
Professional developers spend a lot of time **debugging** — finding and fixing problems. Here's a calm, systematic approach.

### 1. Reproduce the bug
Find the exact steps and inputs that cause the problem. If you can't make it happen reliably, you can't be sure you've fixed it.

### 2. Read the error message
Note the error type and line number. Search the exact message online — someone has almost certainly had the same problem.

### 3. Print what's happening
Add temporary `print()` lines to see the values of variables:

```python
for item in cart:
    print("DEBUG item =", item)      # what is actually in the list?
    total += item["price"] * item["qty"]
```

Often the value isn't what you expected — a string instead of a number, or an empty list.

### 4. Shrink the problem
Comment out parts of the code, or copy the suspicious part into a small new file. The smaller the code, the easier it is to see the bug.

### 5. Rubber duck debugging
Explain your code, line by line, out loud to someone — or to a rubber duck! Saying it aloud often makes the mistake obvious.

### 6. Fix one thing at a time and test again
Change one thing, run the program, and check. Changing many things at once makes it hard to know what worked.

### Logic errors
The hardest bugs produce no error at all — the program runs but gives the wrong answer. For example, using `>` instead of `>=` means a score of exactly 50 fails. Test with **edge cases**: 0, negative numbers, empty input, the exact boundary values.

> [!TRY]
> This code should print the average but doesn't. Find the bug:
> `scores = [70, 80, 90]` then `average = sum(scores) / 2`.

lessons.title: Project — build a quiz game
lessons.content:
Let's combine everything into a complete program: a multiple-choice quiz game with scoring.

### Plan first
1. Store questions, options and answers in a list of dictionaries.
2. Loop through the questions, show options, get the user's answer.
3. Validate input (only a, b, c or d).
4. Keep score and give feedback.
5. Show a final result and a grade.

### The code
```python
# DBI Learn — Python Quiz Game

QUESTIONS = [
    {
        "question": "What is the capital of Ghana?",
        "options": {"a": "Kumasi", "b": "Accra", "c": "Tamale", "d": "Cape Coast"},
        "answer": "b",
    },
    {
        "question": "Which data type stores True or False?",
        "options": {"a": "int", "b": "str", "c": "bool", "d": "float"},
        "answer": "c",
    },
    {
        "question": "What does len('DBI') return?",
        "options": {"a": "2", "b": "3", "c": "4", "d": "DBI"},
        "answer": "b",
    },
]


def ask(q):
    """Show one question and return True if answered correctly."""
    print("\n" + q["question"])
    for letter, text in q["options"].items():
        print(f"  {letter}) {text}")

    while True:
        choice = input("Your answer (a/b/c/d): ").strip().lower()
        if choice in q["options"]:
            break
        print("Please type a, b, c or d.")

    if choice == q["answer"]:
        print("✅ Correct!")
        return True
    correct_text = q["options"][q["answer"]]
    print(f"❌ Not quite. The answer is {q['answer']}) {correct_text}")
    return False


def grade(percent):
    if percent >= 80:
        return "Excellent!"
    if percent >= 50:
        return "Good job!"
    return "Keep practising!"


def main():
    print("=== Welcome to the DBI Quiz ===")
    name = input("What's your name? ").strip() or "Learner"
    score = 0
    for q in QUESTIONS:
        if ask(q):
            score += 1
    percent = round(score / len(QUESTIONS) * 100)
    print(f"\n{name}, you scored {score}/{len(QUESTIONS)} ({percent}%). {grade(percent)}")


main()
```

### Make it your own
- Add at least five more questions on a topic you love.
- Shuffle the questions with `import random` and `random.shuffle(QUESTIONS)`.
- Add a timer using `import time` and `time.time()`.
- Ask "Play again? (y/n)" at the end using a `while` loop.

> [!TIP]
> Notice how each function does one job. This makes the program easy to read, test and extend — the mark of a good programmer.

> [!TRY]
> Complete the quiz game with 10 questions and one extra feature. Share your code in the course discussion!
