lessons.title: What is graphic design?
lessons.content:
**Graphic design** is the art of communicating ideas visually by combining text, images, colour and shapes. A good design isn't just pretty — it gets the right message to the right people quickly.

### Where you see graphic design every day
- Posters for church programmes, school events and concerts
- Product packaging on shop shelves
- Billboards and roadside signs
- Social media posts and WhatsApp status graphics
- Logos of banks, telecoms and football clubs
- Websites and app screens

### Design is communication
Before you open any design tool, answer three questions:

1. **Who** is this for? (students, parents, business owners…)
2. **What** must they understand or do? (attend an event, buy a product, call a number)
3. **Where** will they see it? (a phone screen, a printed A4 poster, a large banner)

A poster for a youth coding workshop and a funeral announcement need very different designs, even though both share dates and venues.

### The design process
1. **Brief** — understand the goal, audience, content and deadline.
2. **Research** — collect inspiration (Pinterest, Behance, Canva templates).
3. **Sketch** — quick rough layouts on paper. Five ugly sketches beat one perfect one.
4. **Design** — build it in your tool.
5. **Feedback** — show someone from the target audience.
6. **Refine and deliver** — fix issues and export the right file.

> [!TIP]
> Professionals collect designs they like in a "swipe file". Start a folder of screenshots of posters and posts that catch your eye, and note *why* each one works.

> [!TRY]
> Find three posters or social media graphics around you. For each, write who it's for, what it wants you to do, and whether it succeeds.

lessons.title: Hierarchy, contrast and alignment
lessons.content:
Three principles do most of the work in any good design.

### Visual hierarchy — what do people see first?
Hierarchy guides the viewer's eye in order of importance. On an event poster the order might be:

1. **Event name** — biggest and boldest
2. **Date, time and venue** — clear and easy to find
3. **Details** — speakers, activities
4. **Call to action / contact** — "Register: 024 000 0000"

Create hierarchy with **size**, **weight** (bold vs regular), **colour**, and **position** (top and centre are seen first).

> [!WARNING]
> If everything is big and bold, nothing stands out. A common beginner mistake is making all text the same size — or every line a different colour.

### Contrast — make important things different
Contrast means making elements clearly different so they stand out:

- **Colour contrast:** dark text on a light background (or the reverse).
- **Size contrast:** a huge headline with small body text.
- **Weight contrast:** a bold heading with light body text.
- **Shape contrast:** one circle among squares.

Contrast is also about **readability**. Light yellow text on a white background is almost invisible — especially for people with weak eyesight or when printed on a cheap printer.

### Alignment — line things up
Every element should line up with something else. Invisible lines create order and make designs feel professional.

- **Left alignment** is easiest to read for paragraphs.
- **Centre alignment** works for short headlines and formal designs but is hard to read for long text.
- Don't mix many alignments in one design — choose one main alignment.

Use the guides and snapping in Canva: the pink lines that appear when you drag an element show it's aligned.

> [!TRY]
> Take a cluttered flyer (or find one online). Redesign it on paper with a clear hierarchy: one dominant headline, then key details, then contact information, all left-aligned.

lessons.title: Repetition, proximity and white space
lessons.content:
### Repetition — create consistency
Repeating colours, fonts, shapes or styles ties a design together and builds a recognisable **brand**. If your headings are green and bold on page one, keep them green and bold on every page, post and poster.

### Proximity — group related things
Items that belong together should be close together; unrelated items should be further apart. On a flyer, keep the date, time and venue as one group, and the contact details as another. Readers then understand the structure without effort.

### White space — let the design breathe
**White space** (or *negative space*) is the empty area around and between elements. It doesn't have to be white — it's simply space without content.

Beginners often try to fill every corner. Professionals do the opposite:

- Space makes designs look **premium and confident**.
- It improves **readability**.
- It directs **attention** to what matters.

Think of luxury brands: lots of space, few words.

### Balance
- **Symmetrical balance** — equal weight on both sides; formal and stable (certificates, invitations).
- **Asymmetrical balance** — different elements balance each other (a big photo on the left balanced by text on the right); dynamic and modern.

### The squint test
Squint at your design until it's blurry. Can you still see the most important element? Are the groups clear? If everything blurs into one grey mass, increase contrast and spacing.

> [!TIP]
> When a design feels "wrong" but you don't know why, try removing something. Often less is more.

> [!TRY]
> Redesign the same flyer from the last lesson using clear groups (proximity) and at least 20% empty space. Compare the before and after.

lessons.title: Typography basics
lessons.content:
**Typography** is the art of arranging text. Because most designs are mostly text, typography often decides whether a design looks amateur or professional.

### Font categories
| Category | Looks like | Feels | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Serif** | Small "feet" on letters (e.g. Times, Playfair, Cormorant) | Traditional, trustworthy, elegant | Certificates, invitations, formal documents |
| **Sans-serif** | Clean, no feet (e.g. Inter, Montserrat, Poppins) | Modern, friendly, clear | Social posts, apps, body text on screens |
| **Script** | Handwriting style (e.g. Great Vibes) | Personal, elegant | Names on certificates, wedding cards — sparingly! |
| **Display** | Decorative, bold | Fun, loud | Big headlines only |

### Golden rules
1. **Use two fonts at most** — one for headings, one for body text. A single font family in different weights also works beautifully.
2. **Pair contrasting fonts** — a bold sans-serif headline with a clean serif body, or vice versa. Two similar fonts together look like a mistake.
3. **Body text must be readable** — never use script or display fonts for paragraphs.
4. **Size matters** — on a social post, the smallest text should still be readable on a phone screen without zooming.
5. **Line spacing** — give lines of body text breathing room (about 1.4–1.6× the font size).
6. **Avoid ALL CAPS** for long text — it's hard to read. Short labels in caps with extra letter spacing can look elegant.

### Good font pairings to try in Canva
- **Montserrat** (headings) + **Open Sans** (body)
- **Playfair Display** (headings) + **Lato** (body)
- **Poppins** Bold + Poppins Regular
- **Anton** (impact headlines) + **Roboto** (body)

> [!WARNING]
> Stretching or squashing text to fit a space distorts the letters. Change the font size instead.

> [!TRY]
> Create a simple quote graphic: the quote in one font and the author's name in another, following the pairing rules above.

lessons.title: Colour theory and palettes
lessons.content:
Colour creates mood, draws attention and builds recognition.

### The colour wheel
- **Primary colours:** red, yellow, blue.
- **Complementary colours:** opposite on the wheel (blue & orange, red & green). High contrast and energetic.
- **Analogous colours:** next to each other (blue, teal, green). Calm and harmonious.
- **Monochromatic:** different shades and tints of one colour. Elegant and simple.

### Colour psychology (in general)
| Colour | Often suggests |
|---|---|
| Green | Growth, nature, health, money |
| Blue | Trust, calm, technology, banks |
| Red | Energy, urgency, passion, sales |
| Yellow / gold | Optimism, attention, luxury (gold) |
| Purple | Creativity, royalty |
| Black | Power, elegance, luxury |

Meanings vary by culture and context. In Ghana, red and black are traditional funeral colours, while white often signals celebration and victory — so think about your audience!

### The 60–30–10 rule
A simple formula for balanced colour:
- **60%** dominant/neutral colour (often white, cream or a dark background)
- **30%** secondary colour
- **10%** accent colour for buttons, highlights and the most important details

### Building a palette
1. Start from the **brand colour** or a photo you're using.
2. Use a palette generator like Coolors or Canva's colour palette tool.
3. Pick 1–2 main colours, 1 accent, plus a light and a dark neutral.
4. Save colour codes (e.g. `#03C14B`) so you can reuse them exactly.

### Accessibility
About 1 in 12 men have some form of colour blindness. Never use colour alone to show meaning (e.g. red/green for wrong/right) — add icons or labels. Check text contrast with a free contrast checker.

> [!TRY]
> Create a five-colour palette for an imaginary juice brand. Label each colour with its role (dominant, secondary, accent, light neutral, dark neutral).

lessons.title: Images, icons and using them legally
lessons.content:
Strong images make designs come alive — but they must be good quality and used legally.

### Image quality
- Use **high-resolution** images. A blurry or pixelated photo instantly makes a design look cheap.
- For print, images should be at least **300 DPI** at the printed size.
- Avoid stretching images out of proportion — hold **Shift** (or use corner handles) to resize evenly.

### Choosing great photos
- Authentic over staged: real people in real settings (and local faces where possible — your audience wants to see themselves).
- One strong focal point.
- Leave space in the photo for text, or place text on a solid shape over the image.

### Text on images
Text placed directly on a busy photo is hard to read. Solutions:
- Add a semi-transparent dark or light **overlay** over the photo.
- Place text on a **solid shape** (rectangle or circle).
- Use the empty area of the photo (sky, wall).

### Using images legally
Just because an image is on Google doesn't mean you can use it. Copyright protects photos, illustrations and logos.

- ✅ Use **free stock** sites: Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay — free for most uses.
- ✅ Use Canva's **free** elements (paid ones show a crown icon).
- ✅ Take your own photos.
- ✅ Get **written permission** for photos of people, especially children, before using them in marketing.
- ❌ Don't copy other brands' logos or artwork.

### Icons and illustrations
Icons make information quick to scan (📍 venue, 📅 date, 📞 phone). Use icons from the **same style family** — mixing cartoon and outline icons looks messy.

> [!TRY]
> Find two free photos on Unsplash or Pexels for a "Back to school" campaign. Place text on one using an overlay and on the other using a solid shape. Which reads better?

lessons.title: Getting started with Canva
lessons.content:
**Canva** is a free online design tool used by millions of individuals and businesses. It runs in a web browser at canva.com and as an app on Android and iPhone. Students and teachers can apply for **Canva for Education**, and NGOs can apply for **Canva for Nonprofits** — both unlock premium features for free.

### Creating a design
1. Sign up with your email or Google account.
2. On the home page, search for a design type: *Instagram Post*, *Flyer (A4)*, *Poster*, *Logo*, *Presentation*. Canva sets the correct size automatically.
3. Or click **Custom size** and enter your own dimensions.

### The editor
- **Left panel** — Templates, Elements (shapes, icons, illustrations), Text, Uploads, Photos, Apps.
- **Canvas** — the middle area where you design.
- **Top toolbar** — changes depending on what's selected: font, colour, effects, position, transparency.

### Essential skills
- **Select** an element by clicking it; **Shift-click** to select several.
- **Group** elements (`Ctrl + G`) so they move together.
- **Align** and **distribute** with **Position** in the toolbar.
- **Layers:** use *Position → Forward/Backward* to bring things in front or behind.
- **Lock** an element so you don't move it by accident.
- **Duplicate** a page to create variations quickly.
- `Ctrl + Z` undo — your safety net.

### Templates: use them wisely
Templates are a great starting point, but thousands of people use the same ones. Always customise them: change the colours to your palette, swap the fonts, replace photos and rearrange the layout. A template should be a starting point, not the finished design.

> [!TIP]
> Turn on **View → Show rulers and guides** to align elements precisely, and use the **margins** setting to keep important content away from the edges.

> [!TRY]
> Create a free Canva account and open a blank Instagram Post (1080 × 1080 px). Add a heading, a shape and an icon, then group and align them in the centre.

lessons.title: Designing a flyer and social media posts
lessons.content:
Let's design a real flyer: **"Free Coding Workshop for Young People"**.

### Step 1 — Gather the content
- Headline: *Learn to Code — Free!*
- Sub-headline: *A 2-day beginner workshop in web development*
- Date & time: *Saturday 14 – Sunday 15 March, 9am – 1pm*
- Venue: *Ayeldu Community Centre*
- Call to action: *Register free: 024 000 0000*
- Logos of organisers and partners

### Step 2 — Choose the format
- **Print:** A4 or A3 portrait. Leave a margin of at least 5 mm from every edge.
- **WhatsApp status / Instagram story:** 1080 × 1920 px (vertical).
- **Instagram / Facebook post:** 1080 × 1080 px (square) or 1080 × 1350 px (portrait).

### Step 3 — Layout
- Put the **headline** in the top third in your boldest font.
- Use a strong photo of young people at computers (with permission!).
- Group **date, time and venue** together with small icons.
- Place the **call to action** at the bottom in a contrasting accent-colour box.
- Logos go in a neat row at the bottom — make them all a similar visual size.

### Step 4 — Design for the phone
Most people will see your design on a small screen while scrolling. Ask yourself:
- Can I read the headline in one second?
- Is the most important text big enough on a phone?
- Is there too much text? Cut ruthlessly — put extra details in the caption instead.

### Step 5 — Create a set
Use **Resize** (Canva Pro) or duplicate and adapt manually to create matching versions: a printed A4 flyer, a square post and a vertical status. Consistent colours, fonts and layout across them all builds recognition.

### Caption tips for social posts
The design grabs attention; the caption gives details. Start with a hook, give the key info, end with a clear action ("Tap the link to register 👇") and add 3–5 relevant hashtags.

> [!TRY]
> Design the coding workshop flyer in A4 and a matching 1080 × 1080 social post. Check both with the squint test.

lessons.title: Designing a simple logo and brand kit
lessons.content:
A **logo** is the face of a brand. A **brand kit** is the set of rules — logo, colours, fonts — that keeps every design consistent.

### What makes a good logo?
- **Simple** — recognisable at a glance and easy to remember.
- **Scalable** — works as a tiny app icon and on a huge banner.
- **Versatile** — works in full colour, in black and white, and on dark backgrounds.
- **Appropriate** — fits the business (a clinic shouldn't look like a nightclub).
- **Timeless** — avoids trendy effects that will look dated next year.

### Types of logos
- **Wordmark** — the name in a distinctive font (e.g. Google).
- **Lettermark** — initials (e.g. DBI).
- **Symbol / icon** — a picture (e.g. Apple).
- **Combination mark** — symbol plus name, like the DBI Learn logo, which combines a growth emblem with the name and tagline.

### Designing a logo in Canva
1. Write down the brand's name, personality (three words, e.g. *friendly, fresh, local*) and audience.
2. Sketch 10 ideas on paper first.
3. In Canva, start with a **Logo** design (500 × 500 px).
4. Choose one or two fonts and a simple shape or icon.
5. Test it small (zoom out until it's the size of a phone icon) and in black and white.
6. Download as **PNG with a transparent background** (Canva Pro) or ask for an **SVG** for printing.

> [!WARNING]
> Many Canva logo templates and elements can't be trademarked because others can use them too. For an important business, customise heavily or work with a designer on an original mark.

### The brand kit
Create a one-page brand guide including:
- Logo versions (full colour, white, black) and minimum size
- Colour palette with exact codes
- Heading and body fonts
- Example of a social post and a flyer using the brand

> [!TRY]
> Create a logo and one-page brand kit for a real or imaginary local business — a chop bar, salon or tailoring shop.

lessons.title: Exporting for print and screen
lessons.content:
The same design must be saved differently depending on where it will be used.

### Screen vs print
| | Screen (social, web, WhatsApp) | Print (posters, flyers, banners) |
|---|---|---|
| Colour mode | **RGB** | **CMYK** (printers use cyan, magenta, yellow, black inks) |
| Resolution | 72–150 PPI is fine | **300 DPI** at final size |
| Formats | PNG, JPG, MP4, GIF | **PDF Print**, high-quality PNG |
| Extra | Keep files small for fast loading | Add **bleed** and crop marks |

### Bleed and safe area
Printers can't print exactly to the edge of the paper. **Bleed** is an extra 3 mm of background beyond the edge that gets trimmed off, so there are no white borders. In Canva: **File → Show print bleed**, extend backgrounds into the bleed, and keep text inside the margin (safe area). When downloading, choose **PDF Print** and tick **Crop marks and bleed**.

### Choosing formats for screen
- **PNG** — sharp text and graphics, supports transparency.
- **JPG** — smaller files for photo-heavy designs.
- **PDF Standard** — documents to share or read on screen.
- **MP4 / GIF** — animated designs.

### Talk to the printer
Before printing many copies, ask the print shop for their preferred file format and bleed size, and print one proof copy first. Colours on paper often look darker than on a bright phone screen.

> [!TRY]
> Export your workshop flyer twice: as a PNG for WhatsApp and as a PDF Print with bleed. Compare the file sizes.

lessons.title: Working with clients and feedback
lessons.content:
Design skills can earn you money — but working with clients needs good communication.

### Start with a clear brief
Ask:
- What is the goal of the design? What should people do after seeing it?
- Who is the audience?
- What text, logos and photos must be included?
- Where will it be used, and in what sizes?
- Are there brand colours or fonts?
- What is the **deadline** and the **budget**?
- Are there examples they like or dislike?

Write the answers down and send a short summary to the client so you both agree.

### Pricing and agreements
- Agree the price, number of **revision rounds** (e.g. two) and delivery date before you start.
- Many designers ask for a **deposit** (for example 50%) before starting.
- State what the client receives: final files in which formats.

### Presenting your work
- Show the design in context — a mockup of the flyer on a wall or the post on a phone screen.
- Explain *why* you made key choices ("The green connects to your brand and stands out on the poster board").
- Offer two or three directions for big projects, not ten.

### Handling feedback professionally
- Listen without taking it personally — feedback is about the design, not you.
- Ask questions: "When you say it should 'pop more', is it the headline or the colours?"
- Push back politely when a change hurts the design's goal, and explain why.
- Keep a record of each version (`flyer-v1`, `flyer-v2`).

> [!TIP]
> Under-promise and over-deliver. Delivering on time, every time, is the fastest way to get repeat clients and referrals.

> [!TRY]
> Write a one-page client brief template you could use for your first real design job.

lessons.title: Building your design portfolio
lessons.content:
A **portfolio** is a collection of your best work. For designers, it matters more than certificates or CVs — clients want to *see* what you can do.

### What to include
- **6–10 of your best pieces** — quality over quantity.
- **Variety:** a flyer, social media set, logo and brand kit, a presentation, maybe a certificate or menu.
- **Context for each piece:** the brief, your process (sketches, versions) and the result. Even practice projects count — label them "concept project".

### Where to show it
- **Behance** — a free platform owned by Adobe, popular with designers worldwide.
- **Instagram** — a dedicated account for your design work.
- **A simple website** — build one with skills from our Web Development course!
- **A PDF portfolio** — 8–12 pages you can attach to emails and WhatsApp.

### Getting your first projects
- Offer to redesign a poster for your school, church or a community group.
- Design for a family member's small business.
- Join design challenges on social media (e.g. 30-day design challenges).
- Volunteer for an NGO — real projects with real impact.

### Keep growing
- Study designs you admire and recreate them for practice (don't publish copies as your own).
- Learn advanced tools later: Adobe Illustrator, Photoshop, or free alternatives like Inkscape, GIMP and Figma.
- Join communities and ask for feedback regularly.

> [!TRY]
> Collect your four best designs from this course into a simple portfolio (a PDF in Canva or a Behance project). Share it in the course discussion for feedback.

course.title: Cybersecurity Basics: Stay Safe Online

course.description:
Cybercrime is growing fast in Ghana and around the world. Criminals steal mobile money, take over WhatsApp and Facebook accounts, and trick people into handing over passwords and personal information. Most attacks succeed not because of clever hacking, but because people don't know the warning signs.

This practical course teaches you how attacks work and exactly what to do to protect yourself, your family and your workplace. It's also the perfect first step if you are curious about a career in cybersecurity — one of the fastest-growing fields in technology.

lessons.title: Why cybersecurity matters
lessons.content:
**Cybersecurity** means protecting computers, phones, networks and data from attack, damage or unauthorised access. As more of life moves online — banking, school, shopping, government services — it affects everyone.

### The CIA triad
Security professionals think about three goals:

| Goal | Meaning | Example of a failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Confidentiality** | Only the right people can see information | Your exam results or medical records are leaked |
| **Integrity** | Information is accurate and hasn't been tampered with | Someone changes the amount on a payment |
| **Availability** | Systems and data work when you need them | A bank's app is down during a cyberattack |

### Who are the attackers?
- **Cybercriminals** — want money: scams, fraud, stealing and selling data, ransomware.
- **Hacktivists** — attack for political or social causes.
- **Insiders** — employees or people you know who misuse their access.
- **State-sponsored groups** — work for governments to spy or disrupt.
- **Opportunists** — not always experts; they use ready-made tools and target easy victims.

### You are a target — even if you're "not important"
Many people think "I have nothing worth stealing." But attackers want:
- your **mobile money and bank balance**,
- your **accounts** (to scam your contacts in your name),
- your **personal data** (to commit identity fraud),
- your **device** (to use in larger attacks).

Most attacks are automated and target thousands of people at once. Good habits make you a harder target, and attackers move on to easier ones.

> [!NOTE]
> Ghana has a **Cyber Security Authority (CSA)** that receives reports of cybercrime. Reporting helps protect others too.

> [!TRY]
> List five online accounts you use (email, MoMo, WhatsApp, social media, school portal). For each, write what an attacker could do if they got access.

lessons.title: Malware, ransomware and how infections happen
lessons.content:
**Malware** (malicious software) is any program designed to harm you or your device.

### Common types of malware
| Type | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Virus** | Attaches to files and spreads when they're shared |
| **Worm** | Spreads by itself across networks |
| **Trojan** | Pretends to be useful software (a "free" game or cracked app) but contains malware |
| **Spyware** | Secretly watches what you do — messages, passwords, location |
| **Adware** | Floods you with ads and slows your device |
| **Ransomware** | Locks or encrypts your files and demands payment to unlock them |

### How devices get infected
- Installing apps from **outside official stores** (APK files shared on WhatsApp or websites)
- Downloading **pirated** software, films or games
- Opening **email attachments** from unknown senders
- Clicking **links** in suspicious messages
- Plugging in **infected flash drives** — very common in shared computer labs and print shops
- Using outdated software with known security holes

### Signs your device might be infected
- Suddenly very slow, hot, or the battery drains quickly
- Pop-up ads everywhere, even outside the browser
- Apps you didn't install
- Data bundle finishing much faster than usual
- Friends receiving strange messages from you

### Ransomware: why backups matter
Ransomware attacks have shut down hospitals, schools and businesses worldwide. Paying doesn't guarantee you'll get your files back. The best protection is **regular backups** stored separately — then you can restore without paying.

> [!WARNING]
> "Cracked" or "free premium" versions of paid apps are one of the most common ways malware spreads. If it's normally paid and someone offers it free, assume there's a catch.

> [!TRY]
> On your phone, open **Settings → Apps** and review the list. Uninstall any app you don't recognise or no longer use.

lessons.title: Social engineering — hacking humans
lessons.content:
**Social engineering** means tricking people into giving away information or doing something unsafe. It's often easier to fool a person than to break into a computer.

### The attacker's psychological tricks
- **Urgency** — "Your account will be blocked in 30 minutes!"
- **Authority** — pretending to be a bank, telecom, police officer, school head or boss.
- **Fear** — "There's a warrant for your arrest unless you pay."
- **Greed / excitement** — "You've won a prize!", "Get rich with this investment."
- **Trust & familiarity** — using a friend's hacked account or knowing your name.
- **Helpfulness** — "I'm from IT support, I need your password to fix your computer."

When you notice any of these feelings being pushed on you, **slow down**. That pressure is a warning sign.

### Common social-engineering attacks
- **Phishing** — fake emails or websites that steal logins (more in the next module).
- **Vishing** — voice phishing: phone calls pretending to be your bank or network.
- **Smishing** — SMS phishing: text messages with fake links or instructions.
- **Pretexting** — inventing a believable story ("I'm the new accountant, please send me the staff list").
- **Baiting** — leaving infected flash drives labelled "Salaries 2026" for someone to plug in.
- **Shoulder surfing** — watching you type your PIN at an ATM or MoMo vendor.

### The golden defence: verify independently
If someone asks for money, a code or information:
1. **Stop** — don't act immediately.
2. **Verify** using a contact you already trust — call the official number on the back of your card, or call your friend on their usual number.
3. **Never** share PINs, passwords or one-time codes. No genuine organisation will ask for them.

> [!TIP]
> Agree a "family password" with close relatives. If someone calls claiming to be them in trouble and asking for money, ask for the password.

> [!TRY]
> Think of a message you or someone you know received that turned out to be a scam. Which psychological tricks did it use?

lessons.title: Strong passwords and password managers
lessons.content:
Weak and reused passwords are behind a huge share of account takeovers.

### How passwords get cracked
- **Guessing** — names, birthdays, phone numbers, football clubs.
- **Brute force** — computers trying billions of combinations; short passwords fall in seconds.
- **Dictionary attacks** — trying common words and leaked passwords (`password123`, `iloveyou`).
- **Credential stuffing** — using passwords leaked from one website to log in to others. This is why **reusing passwords is so dangerous**.

### What makes a password strong?
**Length beats complexity.** A long passphrase is both stronger and easier to remember than a short jumble.

| Password | Rough time to crack |
|---|---|
| `kofi1995` | Instantly (name + year) |
| `K0f!95` | Minutes to hours |
| `Banku-Lantern-Rocket-River` | Centuries |

Guidelines:
- At least **12–16 characters**; a passphrase of **4 random words** is great.
- **Unique** for every important account.
- Never based on personal information others can find.

### Password managers
A **password manager** stores all your passwords in an encrypted vault, protected by one strong master password. It can generate random passwords and fill them in for you.

- Free options: **Bitwarden**, and the password managers built into **Google Chrome/Android** and **Apple** devices.
- You only need to remember **one** strong master passphrase.

### Check for leaks
Visit **haveibeenpwned.com** and enter your email to see whether it appeared in known data breaches. If it has, change the password for that site — and anywhere you reused it.

> [!WARNING]
> Writing your PIN on your MoMo SIM pack or phone case, or sharing it with a vendor "to help", gives criminals easy access.

> [!TRY]
> Check your email on haveibeenpwned.com. Then create a four-word passphrase and use it for your most important account.

lessons.title: Multi-factor authentication
lessons.content:
**Multi-factor authentication (MFA)** — also called two-factor or two-step verification — requires a second proof of identity in addition to your password.

### The three factors
1. **Something you know** — password, PIN
2. **Something you have** — your phone, a security key
3. **Something you are** — fingerprint, face

Using two different factors means a stolen password alone isn't enough.

### Types of second factor (from weaker to stronger)
- **SMS codes** — better than nothing, but vulnerable to SIM-swap fraud.
- **Authenticator apps** (Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator) — generate codes on your phone; stronger than SMS.
- **Passkeys and security keys** — the strongest option; resistant to phishing.

### Turn it on now
- **Email (Gmail/Outlook):** Account settings → Security → 2-Step Verification. Do this first — your email can reset all your other passwords.
- **WhatsApp:** Settings → Account → Two-step verification → set a 6-digit PIN.
- **Facebook / Instagram:** Settings → Accounts Center → Password and security → Two-factor authentication.
- **Mobile money / banking apps:** enable biometrics and keep your PIN secret.

Save your **backup codes** somewhere safe (on paper, at home) in case you lose your phone.

### SIM-swap fraud
Criminals convince or bribe someone to transfer your phone number to a new SIM card. They then receive your SMS codes and MoMo access. Warning sign: your phone suddenly shows "No service" for a long time. Contact your network immediately.

> [!TIP]
> Any time you receive a login code you didn't request, someone may know your password. Change it immediately.

> [!TRY]
> Turn on two-step verification for your email and WhatsApp today, and store your backup codes safely.

lessons.title: Recognising phishing
lessons.content:
**Phishing** is when attackers pretend to be a trusted organisation to trick you into revealing information or clicking a malicious link. It's the most common cyberattack in the world.

### Anatomy of a phishing message
```
From: MTN MoMo Security <momo-alert@mtn-secure-verify.com>
Subject: URGENT: Your MoMo wallet will be suspended

Dear Customer,

We detected unusual activity on your account. To avoid suspension
within 24 hours, verify your details now:

https://mtn-momo-verify.gh-login.net

Enter your number and PIN to continue.
```

Red flags:
- 🚩 The sender's domain isn't the real company domain.
- 🚩 Generic greeting: "Dear Customer".
- 🚩 Urgency and threats: "within 24 hours".
- 🚩 A link to a strange domain — the real domain is the part just before the first single `/`. Here it's `gh-login.net`, not MTN.
- 🚩 It asks for your **PIN** — legitimate companies never do.
- 🚩 Spelling or grammar mistakes (but modern phishing can be well written!).

### Check links before you click
- On a computer, **hover** over a link to see where it really goes.
- On a phone, **long-press** the link to preview the address.
- When in doubt, don't click. Open the official app or type the website address yourself.

### Spear phishing
Some attacks are personalised using information from your social media: your name, school, boss's name. These are harder to spot — another reason to keep personal information private.

### What to do with a phishing message
1. Don't click links, download attachments or reply.
2. Report it (in Gmail: **⋮ → Report phishing**; forward scam SMS to your network's reporting number).
3. Delete it.
4. If you already entered a password, **change it immediately** and turn on MFA.

> [!TRY]
> Look at your email spam folder. Find one phishing message and identify at least three red flags.

lessons.title: Securing phones and computers
lessons.content:
Your phone holds your money, messages, photos and identity. Protect it like your wallet.

### Essential device protections
1. **Screen lock** — use a 6-digit PIN or biometrics (fingerprint/face). Simple swipe patterns are easy to guess from smudges on the screen. Never leave your phone unlocked.
2. **Updates** — install system and app updates promptly. They fix security holes that attackers actively exploit.
3. **Official app stores only** — Google Play or the Apple App Store. Turn off "Install unknown apps".
4. **App permissions** — does a torch app really need your contacts and location? Review permissions in Settings and remove unnecessary ones.
5. **Find My Device** — turn on Google's *Find My Device* or Apple's *Find My* so you can locate, lock or erase a lost phone.
6. **Antivirus** — on Windows, keep **Microsoft Defender** switched on (it's built in and free). On Android, Google Play Protect scans apps.
7. **Encryption** — modern phones encrypt data automatically when you set a screen lock.

### Shared and public computers
In internet cafés, libraries and school labs:
- Use a **private/incognito** window.
- Never tick "Remember me" or let the browser save your password.
- Always **log out** and close the browser when done.
- Avoid banking or MoMo on shared computers.

### Flash drives
Scan flash drives with antivirus before opening files, especially ones used at print shops. Never plug in a drive you found lying around.

### If your phone is lost or stolen
1. Use Find My Device to lock or erase it.
2. Call your network provider to **block the SIM** (this protects your MoMo).
3. Change passwords for email and important apps.
4. Report to the police if stolen.

> [!TRY]
> Check that your phone has a screen lock, Find My Device is on, and all updates are installed. Review the permissions of three apps.

lessons.title: Safe browsing and public Wi-Fi
lessons.content:
### HTTPS and the padlock
Websites starting with `https://` encrypt data between you and the site. Never enter passwords or payment details on a page without HTTPS. But remember: the padlock means the *connection* is private — **not** that the website is honest. Scammers can get padlocks too.

### Public Wi-Fi risks
Free Wi-Fi in hotels, airports and cafés is convenient but risky:
- Attackers can create **fake hotspots** with names like "Free_Airport_WiFi".
- On poorly secured networks, others may be able to see unencrypted traffic.

Safer habits:
- Avoid banking, MoMo and entering passwords on public Wi-Fi — use your mobile data instead.
- Confirm the exact network name with staff.
- Turn off **auto-connect** to open networks.
- A reputable **VPN** encrypts your traffic on public networks.

### Your home Wi-Fi
- Change the router's default admin password.
- Use **WPA2** or **WPA3** security with a strong Wi-Fi password.
- Update the router's software when available.

### Downloads and pop-ups
- Download software only from official websites.
- Close pop-ups that say "Your phone has a virus! Click here" — they're scams.
- Be careful with browser extensions; install only well-known ones.

> [!TIP]
> Bookmark the real websites of your bank and school portal, and always use the bookmark instead of searching or clicking links.

> [!TRY]
> Check your phone's Wi-Fi settings and turn off automatic connection to open networks.

lessons.title: Privacy and your digital footprint
lessons.content:
**Privacy** is your right to control who knows what about you. Every post, check-in, like and app sign-up adds to your **digital footprint**.

### What attackers can learn from social media
- Your full name, school, workplace and friends
- Your birthday (often used in passwords and security questions)
- Your location and daily routine (photos tagged at home, "Travelling to Accra today!")
- Your family members' names
- Your phone number and email

Combined, this information enables **identity theft**, convincing **spear-phishing**, and even physical risks.

### Privacy checklist for social media
- ✅ Set your profile to **private** or **friends only**.
- ✅ Hide your phone number and email from your public profile.
- ✅ Turn off location tagging on photos.
- ✅ Post holiday photos *after* you return, not while your home is empty.
- ✅ Don't post photos of ID cards, certificates with ID numbers, boarding passes or bank cards.
- ✅ Review which apps are connected to your Facebook or Google account and remove unused ones.
- ✅ Think before sharing others' photos and information — get consent.

### Data protection law
Ghana's **Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843)** gives people rights over their personal data and requires organisations to protect it. Organisations should collect only what they need and keep it secure — something to remember if you build apps or run a business.

### Quizzes and "fun" apps
Viral quizzes like "Your stage name is your first pet + street you grew up on" are often harvesting answers to common security questions. Skip them.

> [!TRY]
> Open the privacy settings of one social media account and make three changes that reduce what strangers can see.

lessons.title: What to do if you've been hacked or scammed
lessons.content:
Even careful people can be caught. Acting quickly limits the damage.

### If an account is hacked
1. **Try to recover it** — use the "Forgot password" option or the platform's account recovery page.
2. **Change the password** to a new, unique one.
3. **Turn on MFA** and remove unknown devices and sessions (Settings → Security → Devices).
4. **Check recovery details** — make sure the recovery email and phone number are yours.
5. **Warn your contacts** that messages from your account may be fake.
6. **Change reused passwords** on other sites.

### If you've lost money to a scam
1. **Call your network or bank immediately** — mobile money providers can sometimes freeze or reverse transactions if reported quickly.
2. **Collect evidence** — screenshots, phone numbers, transaction IDs, dates.
3. **Report to the police** and to Ghana's **Cyber Security Authority** (CSA).
4. Be careful of "recovery scams" — people who promise to get your money back for a fee.

### If your device may be infected
1. Disconnect from the internet.
2. Run a full antivirus scan.
3. Uninstall suspicious apps.
4. If problems continue, back up personal files (photos, documents — not apps) and **factory reset** the device.

### At work or school
Report incidents to the IT team or a teacher right away — even if you think you made a mistake. Quick reporting can stop an attack spreading. Good organisations treat reporting as responsible, not shameful.

> [!TIP]
> Save your network's customer care number and your bank's official fraud line in your contacts now, before you ever need them.

> [!TRY]
> Write a one-page "If I get hacked" plan with the steps and phone numbers you would need. Keep a copy at home.

lessons.title: Security at work and for small businesses
lessons.content:
Businesses, schools and NGOs hold valuable data: customer details, payments, staff records. Small organisations are frequent targets because they often have weaker defences.

### Key practices for organisations
- **Least privilege** — give each person access only to what they need for their job.
- **Strong authentication** — MFA on email and admin accounts.
- **Regular backups** — automated, tested, with a copy offline or off-site.
- **Updates** — keep all computers, phones and the website updated.
- **Security awareness training** — teach staff to spot phishing; people are the first line of defence.
- **Separate accounts** — don't share logins between staff; remove access when people leave.
- **Payment verification** — confirm any change of supplier bank or MoMo details by phone using a known number. "Invoice fraud" emails often ask to pay a "new account".

### Protecting customer data
- Collect only what you need.
- Store it securely; don't leave customer lists on shared computers or open WhatsApp groups.
- Follow the Data Protection Act.

### Simple policies
Even a small business should write down:
- Who can access which systems.
- How passwords and devices must be protected.
- What to do and who to call when something goes wrong.

> [!TRY]
> Imagine you run a small shop that takes mobile money and has a WhatsApp business account. List the top five security measures you would put in place.

lessons.title: Careers in cybersecurity
lessons.content:
Cybersecurity has a big global skills shortage — millions of unfilled jobs worldwide — and demand in Africa is growing quickly as banks, telecoms, fintechs and governments go digital.

### Roles in cybersecurity
- **Security Analyst / SOC Analyst** — monitors systems for attacks and responds to alerts.
- **Penetration Tester (ethical hacker)** — legally attacks systems to find weaknesses before criminals do.
- **Security Engineer** — designs and builds secure systems and networks.
- **Incident Responder** — investigates and contains attacks.
- **Governance, Risk & Compliance (GRC)** — creates policies and ensures laws and standards are followed.
- **Security Awareness Trainer** — teaches people to stay safe (like this course!).

### Skills to build
- **Networking** — how the internet and networks work (see our Networking & Cloud course).
- **Operating systems** — Windows and Linux.
- **Programming/scripting** — Python is widely used in security.
- **Curiosity and ethics** — security professionals must be trustworthy.

### Learning pathway
1. Strengthen IT fundamentals (this course, networking, Linux basics).
2. Take free courses such as **Cisco Networking Academy's Introduction to Cybersecurity**.
3. Practise legally on training platforms and capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges designed for learning.
4. Consider entry-level certifications such as CompTIA Security+ or ISC2 Certified in Cybersecurity (CC).

> [!WARNING]
> Only ever test systems you own or have **written permission** to test. Unauthorised hacking is illegal under Ghana's Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038), even if you "don't do any damage".

> [!TRY]
> Research one cybersecurity role that interests you. Write down three skills it needs and one free resource to start learning.

lessons.title: What is digital marketing?
lessons.content:
**Marketing** is the process of understanding what people need and communicating how your product, service or cause meets that need. **Digital marketing** does this through digital channels: social media, search engines, websites, email, messaging apps and online ads.

### Traditional vs digital marketing
| Traditional | Digital |
|---|---|
| Radio, TV, newspapers, billboards, flyers | Social media, search, websites, WhatsApp, email |
| Often expensive | Can start for free; ads can start small |
| Hard to measure who saw it | Detailed data on views, clicks and sales |
| One-way message | Two-way conversation with customers |
| Broad audience | Precise targeting (location, age, interests) |

Both still matter — a radio ad plus a strong Facebook page often works better than either alone.

### The main digital channels
- **Social media** — Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), LinkedIn, YouTube.
- **Messaging** — WhatsApp (hugely popular in Ghana), Telegram.
- **Search engines** — Google; people searching for what you offer *right now*.
- **Websites and online stores** — your own space online.
- **Email and SMS** — direct communication with customers who opted in.
- **Online marketplaces** — Jumia, Tonaton and others.

### Owned, earned and paid media
- **Owned** — channels you control: your page, website, WhatsApp catalogue, email list.
- **Earned** — free attention: shares, reviews, word of mouth, news stories.
- **Paid** — ads and sponsored posts.

Build owned channels first — they're yours, even if an algorithm changes.

> [!TRY]
> Pick a local business you know. List which digital channels it uses now and two channels it should add.

lessons.title: Know your audience
lessons.content:
The biggest marketing mistake is trying to reach "everyone". When you speak to everyone, you connect with no one. Instead, define your **target audience**.

### Creating a customer persona
A **persona** is a short profile of your ideal customer. Example for a shop selling affordable school bags:

> **Name:** Auntie Efua
> **Age:** 38, mother of three
> **Location:** Cape Coast
> **Job:** Trader at the market
> **Goals:** Durable bags that last the whole school year, good value
> **Frustrations:** Bags that tear after two months; no time to travel to Accra
> **Online habits:** WhatsApp all day, Facebook in the evening, watches TikTok videos
> **Decides by:** Recommendations from other parents, seeing the product in videos

Now you know where to market (WhatsApp, Facebook, TikTok), what to say (durability, value, delivery), and when (evenings, before school terms start).

### Questions to ask about your audience
- Who are they? (age, location, occupation, language)
- What problems do they have that you solve?
- Where do they spend time online?
- What makes them trust a business?
- What stops them from buying? (price, trust, distance)

### Research methods
- Talk to 5–10 existing customers.
- Look at comments on competitors' pages.
- Run a simple poll on WhatsApp status or Instagram Stories.
- Check Facebook and Instagram Insights to see who follows you.

### Your value proposition
Finish this sentence: *"We help [audience] to [benefit] by [what makes you different]."*

Example: *"We help busy parents in Cape Coast get strong, affordable school bags delivered to their door in 24 hours."*

> [!TRY]
> Write a customer persona and a one-sentence value proposition for a real or imaginary business.

lessons.title: Goals and the marketing funnel
lessons.content:
### The marketing funnel
Customers go through stages before buying:

1. **Awareness** — they discover you exist. (A TikTok video, a shared post.)
2. **Interest** — they want to know more. (They follow your page, visit your profile.)
3. **Consideration** — they compare options. (They read reviews, check prices, message you.)
4. **Conversion** — they buy, register or donate.
5. **Loyalty & advocacy** — they come back and recommend you.

Different content works at each stage: fun, shareable videos for awareness; product details and testimonials for consideration; offers and easy ordering for conversion; thank-you messages and loyalty rewards for retention.

### SMART goals
Vague goals like "get more followers" don't help you plan. Make goals **SMART**:

- **S**pecific — what exactly?
- **M**easurable — how will you know?
- **A**chievable — realistic with your time and budget?
- **R**elevant — does it help the business?
- **T**ime-bound — by when?

❌ "Sell more bags."
✅ "Receive 50 WhatsApp orders for school bags between 1 and 31 August by posting daily product videos on TikTok and Facebook."

### Key metrics (KPIs)
- **Reach** — how many people saw your content
- **Engagement** — likes, comments, shares, saves
- **Click-through rate (CTR)** — % of people who clicked your link
- **Conversions** — orders, sign-ups, enquiries
- **Cost per result** — for paid ads, how much each result costs

Followers are nice, but **sales and enquiries** pay the bills.

> [!TRY]
> Write two SMART goals for your business: one for awareness and one for conversions.

lessons.title: Choosing the right platforms
lessons.content:
You don't need to be everywhere. It's better to be excellent on two platforms than weak on six.

### Platform guide
| Platform | Best for | Content that works |
|---|---|---|
| **WhatsApp** | Direct customer contact, orders, updates | Status updates, catalogues, broadcast lists |
| **Facebook** | Broad local audiences, community groups, events | Photos, videos, events, community posts |
| **Instagram** | Visual products: fashion, food, beauty, design | Reels, high-quality photos, Stories |
| **TikTok** | Reaching new, young audiences fast | Short, authentic, entertaining videos |
| **YouTube** | Tutorials, long-form content, search | How-to videos, reviews |
| **LinkedIn** | Professional services, B2B, careers | Expertise, case studies, company news |
| **X (Twitter)** | News, conversations, customer service | Short updates, trends, replies |

### How to choose
1. Where is your **target audience**? (Look back at your persona.)
2. What **content** can you realistically create? (Photos? Videos? Articles?)
3. How much **time** do you have? Video platforms need more effort but reach more people.

### Optimise your profile
- Clear **profile photo** (your logo) and **cover image**.
- A **bio** that explains what you do, where and how to order: *"Strong, stylish school bags 🎒 | Cape Coast | Delivery in 24h | WhatsApp 024 000 0000"*.
- **Link** to your WhatsApp, website or catalogue.
- Use the same name/handle across platforms so people can find you.

> [!TIP]
> On Facebook and Instagram, switch to a **professional/business account** for free access to Insights (analytics) and contact buttons.

> [!TRY]
> Choose two main platforms for your business and write an optimised bio for each.

lessons.title: Creating engaging content
lessons.content:
Great content either **educates**, **entertains**, **inspires** or **helps** — ideally more than one.

### Content ideas that work
- **Behind the scenes** — how your product is made, your team at work.
- **How-to / tips** — "3 ways to style one kaba", "How to make your school bag last all year".
- **Customer stories and testimonials** — with permission.
- **Before and after** — hair, renovations, designs.
- **Product showcases** — features, prices, colours (always show the price — people hate asking).
- **Questions and polls** — "Which colour should we restock: red or blue?"
- **Trends and challenges** — join relevant trending sounds or topics, with your own twist.
- **Offers** — limited-time discounts, bundles, free delivery days.

### The 80/20 rule
About **80%** of your content should give value (help, entertain, inform) and **20%** should directly sell. If every post says "Buy now!", people stop paying attention.

### Short video is king
Reels, TikToks and WhatsApp status videos get the most reach. Tips:
- **Hook in the first 2 seconds** — start with movement, a question or a surprising result.
- Film **vertically** (9:16).
- Keep it **15–45 seconds**.
- Use good **natural light** (face a window) and clear sound.
- Add **captions** — many people watch without sound.
- End with a **call to action**: "Send us a WhatsApp to order 👇".

### Writing good captions
- First line = hook.
- Short paragraphs and line breaks.
- Clear call to action.
- 3–5 relevant hashtags, mixing popular and local ones (#AccraFood, #MadeInGhana).
- Write in the language your audience uses — English, Twi, Pidgin or a mix.

### Plan with a content calendar
Plan a week or month ahead in a simple spreadsheet: date, platform, content idea, caption, status. **Consistency beats intensity** — three good posts a week, every week, beats ten posts one week and nothing the next.

> [!TRY]
> Plan one week of content (five posts) for your business in a table using the 80/20 rule. Film one short video using the tips above.

lessons.title: Community management and engagement
lessons.content:
Social media is *social*. Brands that talk with their audience build loyal customers.

### Respond quickly
- Reply to comments and messages **within a few hours** — slow replies lose sales.
- Use WhatsApp Business **quick replies** and Facebook **saved replies** for common questions (price, location, delivery).
- Thank people who share or tag you.

### Handle complaints professionally
Every business gets complaints. Handle them well and they can become loyal customers.

1. **Respond publicly and politely** — others are watching how you behave.
2. **Apologise and acknowledge**: "We're sorry your order arrived late, Kojo."
3. **Move to private** to sort details: "We've sent you a WhatsApp message to fix this."
4. **Fix it** and follow up.
5. **Never argue** or delete reasonable criticism.

### Encourage user-generated content
Ask happy customers to post photos with your product and tag you. Reshare them (with permission). Real customers are more persuasive than any ad.

### Work with influencers
Influencers with smaller but loyal local audiences (**micro-influencers**, e.g. 5,000–50,000 followers) are often more affordable and more trusted than celebrities. Choose people whose audience matches your persona, agree clear terms, and make sure sponsored posts are labelled as ads.

### Grow a community
Facebook groups and WhatsApp communities can build loyal followings — for example, a "Cape Coast Parents' Tips" group sponsored by your school bag shop.

> [!TRY]
> Write a polite public reply to this comment: *"I ordered on Monday and still haven't received anything. Very disappointing!"*

lessons.title: WhatsApp Business and Google Business Profile
lessons.content:
### WhatsApp Business
**WhatsApp Business** is a free app designed for small businesses. Install it from your app store (you can use a separate number from your personal WhatsApp).

Key features:
- **Business profile** — address, opening hours, description, email, website.
- **Catalogue** — show products with photos, prices and descriptions. Customers can browse and send orders without leaving the chat.
- **Quick replies** — type `/price` to send a saved answer instantly.
- **Greeting message** — automatic welcome when someone messages you for the first time.
- **Away message** — automatic reply outside business hours.
- **Labels** — organise chats: *New customer, Order placed, Paid, Delivered*.
- **Status** — post daily products and offers that all your contacts can see.
- **Broadcast lists** — send a message to many customers at once (they only receive it if they saved your number).

> [!WARNING]
> Only message people who agreed to hear from you. Spamming strangers gets your number reported and banned.

### Google Business Profile
When people search "printing shop near me" or "salon in Ho", Google shows a map with local businesses. A free **Google Business Profile** puts you on that map.

1. Go to google.com/business and sign in.
2. Add your business name, category, location (or service area), phone and hours.
3. Verify your business (Google will guide you).
4. Add good photos of your shop, products and team.
5. Ask happy customers to leave **reviews** — and reply to every review.

Customers can then call you, get directions and see your reviews directly from Google Search and Maps.

> [!TRY]
> Set up a WhatsApp Business profile (or plan one on paper): write the description, greeting message, away message and three quick replies.

lessons.title: SEO and websites
lessons.content:
**SEO (Search Engine Optimisation)** is the practice of making your website appear higher in Google's free (organic) results.

### How Google ranks pages (simplified)
Google wants to show the most **helpful, relevant and trustworthy** answer for each search. It looks at:
- **Relevance** — does the page match what the person searched?
- **Quality** — is the content useful, original and up to date?
- **Authority** — do other reputable sites link to it?
- **Experience** — does the page load fast and work well on phones?

### Keyword research
**Keywords** are the words people type into Google. Think like your customer:
- "affordable school bags Cape Coast"
- "how to start a poultry farm in Ghana"
- "web designer in Kumasi"

Use Google's autocomplete suggestions and the "People also ask" box for ideas. Longer, more specific phrases (**long-tail keywords**) are easier to rank for.

### On-page SEO basics
- Put the main keyword in the **page title** and **main heading (H1)**.
- Write a clear **meta description** (the summary shown in Google results).
- Create genuinely useful content that answers questions.
- Use descriptive **image alt text**.
- Make sure the site is **fast** and **mobile-friendly**.
- Link to your other relevant pages.

### Local SEO
For local businesses, the Google Business Profile, reviews and consistent name/address/phone across the web matter most.

> [!TIP]
> A simple website you control, with your products, prices, location and WhatsApp button, builds trust — and you can build one yourself with our Web Development course.

> [!TRY]
> List ten keywords your ideal customers might search to find your business. Mark which are "long-tail".

lessons.title: Email marketing and paid ads
lessons.content:
### Email marketing
Social media platforms control who sees your posts. Your **email list** is yours. Email works especially well for B2B services, education programmes, NGOs and online stores.

- Build your list with a reason to subscribe: a free guide, discount or newsletter.
- Only email people who **opted in**, and always include an **unsubscribe** link.
- Free tools like **Mailchimp** or **MailerLite** have free plans for small lists.
- Write a clear subject line, personalise with the reader's name, and include one main call to action.

### Paid social ads
Facebook, Instagram and TikTok ads let you reach people beyond your followers with precise targeting.

**Meta (Facebook/Instagram) ads basics:**
1. Choose an **objective**: Awareness, Traffic, Engagement, Leads, Sales — or **Messages** (great for WhatsApp orders).
2. Define your **audience**: location (e.g. within 10 km of Kumasi), age, interests.
3. Set a **budget** and **schedule** — you can start with a small daily budget.
4. Create the **ad**: a strong image or short video, a clear headline and call-to-action button.
5. **Launch, measure and adjust.**

**Boosting** an existing post is the simplest option; **Ads Manager** gives more control.

### Ad tips
- Test two versions (an **A/B test**) with different images or headlines and keep the winner.
- Video ads usually perform better than plain images.
- Target narrowly at first; expand when you find what works.
- Watch **cost per result** — not just likes.

### Google Ads
Google Ads show your business when people search specific keywords — ideal because the person is already looking for what you sell. You pay when someone clicks (**pay-per-click**).

> [!WARNING]
> Don't spend money on ads before your profile, content and order process are ready. Ads amplify what you have — good or bad.

> [!TRY]
> Plan a small Facebook ad: write the objective, audience (location, age, interests), daily budget, and the headline and text of your ad.

lessons.title: Analytics — measuring what matters
lessons.content:
Digital marketing's superpower is that you can **measure** results and improve.

### Where to find your data
- **Meta Business Suite / Instagram Insights** — reach, engagement, follower demographics, best posting times.
- **TikTok Analytics** — views, watch time, audience.
- **WhatsApp Business** — basic message statistics.
- **Google Business Profile** — searches, calls, direction requests.
- **Google Analytics** — website visitors and what they do.

### Key questions to ask every month
1. Which **posts** got the most reach and engagement? Why?
2. Which **days and times** perform best?
3. Where are **enquiries and sales** coming from?
4. Are we moving toward our **SMART goals**?
5. What should we **do more of** — and stop doing?

### Engagement rate
Likes alone can mislead. **Engagement rate** compares interactions to reach:

```
Engagement rate = (likes + comments + shares + saves) ÷ reach × 100
```

A post with 1,000 reach and 50 interactions has a 5% engagement rate — better than a post with 10,000 reach and 100 interactions (1%).

### Track sales sources
Ask every new customer: *"How did you hear about us?"* and record it in a simple spreadsheet. Use special codes ("Mention TIKTOK10 for 10% off") or separate WhatsApp links to see which channel brings orders.

> [!TIP]
> Make a monthly one-page report: top three posts, key numbers vs last month, and three actions for next month. This is exactly what employers and clients want from a digital marketer.

> [!TRY]
> Calculate the engagement rate for a post with 2,400 reach, 96 likes, 18 comments, 6 shares and 10 saves.

lessons.title: Ethics, trust and the law
lessons.content:
Trust is a business's most valuable asset. Honest marketing builds it; deceptive marketing destroys it — fast.

### Be honest
- Don't make false claims ("cures all diseases", "guaranteed 100% profit").
- Show real prices and fees — no hidden charges.
- Use real photos of your products, not misleading images from the internet.
- Don't buy fake followers or reviews — platforms detect them, and they don't buy anything.

### Respect privacy and consent
- Only add people to broadcast lists or email lists with permission.
- Protect customer data (phone numbers, addresses) — Ghana's Data Protection Act applies to businesses.
- Ask permission before posting photos of customers, and be especially careful with children.

### Disclose sponsorships
If an influencer is paid or gets free products, the post should clearly say so (e.g. #ad, "Paid partnership"). Hidden ads mislead audiences.

### Respect copyright
Use music, images and videos you have the rights to. Platforms provide licensed music libraries for business accounts.

### Be culturally aware
Avoid content that mocks groups of people, religions or tribes. Check that jokes and trends are appropriate for your brand and audience. A single offensive post can go viral for the wrong reasons.

> [!TRY]
> Review three ads or promotional posts you've seen recently. Do any make claims that seem exaggerated or misleading?

lessons.title: Project — your digital marketing plan
lessons.content:
Bring everything together in a one-page **digital marketing plan** for a real or imaginary business.

### Template
**1. Business summary**
What you sell, where, and your value proposition.

**2. Target audience**
Your customer persona (age, location, needs, online habits).

**3. SMART goals**
Two or three goals with numbers and deadlines.

**4. Channels**
Your two or three main platforms and why — for example WhatsApp Business (orders), TikTok (awareness), Google Business Profile (local search).

**5. Content plan**
Content themes (e.g. tips, behind-the-scenes, testimonials, offers), posting frequency, and a sample week.

**6. Tools**
WhatsApp Business, Canva (design), CapCut (video editing), Meta Business Suite (scheduling).

**7. Budget**
Free activities and any paid ads (e.g. GH₵X per week for two weeks to test a Messages campaign).

**8. Measurement**
Which metrics you'll track weekly and monthly, and how you'll know you succeeded.

### Example goal and actions
*Goal:* 60 WhatsApp orders for school bags in August.
*Actions:* daily TikTok/Reels showing durability tests; WhatsApp status every morning; Facebook post in two parents' groups weekly (with admin permission); a two-week Messages ad targeting parents within 15 km; a "Back-to-school bundle" offer in the last week of August.
*Measure:* orders per week, cost per WhatsApp conversation, top-performing video.

> [!TIP]
> A clear plan like this is a powerful portfolio piece. Many small businesses would happily pay a young marketer who can run it for them.

> [!TRY]
> Complete your one-page marketing plan and share it in the course discussion for feedback.

Every time you send a WhatsApp message, pay with mobile money or join a video lesson, your data travels through dozens of networks and data centres in a fraction of a second. Networks and the cloud are the invisible infrastructure of modern life.
